Your pattern is fine — the problem is that those two files are **already tracked**. `.gitignore` only stops git from picking up *untracked* files; once a file has been committed, git keeps reporting its modifications no matter what `.gitignore` says.

You can see both halves of that here:

- `git ls-files agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c12/` → lists both files, so they're in the index (committed at some point before you added the rule).
- `git check-ignore -v --no-index …` → matches `.gitignore:66: agent/impls/s04*/` for both files, so the pattern itself works. Plain `git check-ignore` returns nothing precisely because tracked files are exempt from ignore rules.

To make the rule take effect, untrack them while keeping your local copies:

```bash
git rm -r --cached agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c12/
git commit -m "untrack s04 impl artifacts"
```

After that commit they'll disappear from `git status` and the `s04*/` rule covers them going forward. One caveat: the commit deletes the files from the repo, so any other clone that pulls it will have its checked-out copies removed — if you want them preserved elsewhere, they'd need their own backup. (The local-only alternative is `git update-index --skip-worktree <files>`, which keeps them in the repo but hides your local edits — it tends to bite during pulls/rebases, so I'd only use it if you specifically want the committed versions to stay.)

Same story applies to any other already-committed files under `agent/impls/s04*/` — untracked ones (like new result files) are being ignored correctly already.

ok again we are he "copy-per-draft" confusion â it is NOT the model, and it is NOT one-time

- The model's weights are loaded once at startup and never copied again. Agreed, one-time, excluded. That's not this.
- What gets copied is the input's attention memory (KV cache): after reading a 16k-token prompt, the model keeps ~2 GB of per-token memory that every subsequent step re-reads.
- To check 8 draft states in one batched pass, the lazy implementation calls the standard attention API â which requires each batch row to carry its own memory. So it materializes 8 identical copies of that 2 GB (16 GB!) and streams through all of them. And verification happens at every step of generation, hundreds of times per answer â so this copying/re-reading tax is paid continuously, not once. That's why it measured 3â6Ã and ran out of memory at 32k.
- Why anyone writes it that way: it's the one-line way to batch with stock attention kernels (repeat the memory). It's the natural first implementation â FreeDave ships it as one of two modes.
- The tree mode keeps one copy and lets all 8 drafts read it through a masked attention pattern â same math, bit-identical outputs, â the cost of a single pass. That's the whole

This is the critical distinction — now confirmed from source (lines 1433/1491): the recompute label maps to two independent knobs, `USE_UNSLOTH_GC` and `UNSLOTH_GC_RECOMPUTE_SAVE_ON_CPU`:

- **`recomp`** = plain gradient-checkpoint recompute (no unsloth GC)

[2026-07-17T21:00:51.582Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Explored it — concise verdict:

**What Megatron has** (`third_party/megatron-lm/megatron/core/pipeline_parallel/fine_grained_activation_offload.py`, 1318 lines, config flag `fine_grained_activation_offloading`):
- Dedicated `d2h`/`h2d` CUDA streams + per-group events, pinned CPU backups, prefetch on reload (lines 412-413, 759-772, 902)
- **`GPUTensorPool`** — pre-allocated, shape-keyed, *recycled* GPU + pinned-CPU buffers (line 98) → allocations are deterministic ("regular"), bypassing the torch caching allocator per step
- Tag-grouped tensors (`OffloadTensorGroup`) with a bounded resident window managed by `PipelineOffloadManager`

**Does it mediate thrash? Yes for one half, no for the other:**
1. **Yes — the allocator half.** Our measured thrash is torch-caching-allocator churn near the ceiling (c12's 1.6–1.7× blowups at 98%; asym b5's 62 GiB resv-vs-alloc fragmentation gap). Megatron's pooled/recycled buffers + fixed schedule attack exactly that mechanism — you'd get flat, predictable HBM and could safely run closer to 100% without the blowup. Adopting just the `GPUTensorPool` pattern for asym's reload buffers is a plausible, cheap fix for our fragmentation gap.
2. **No — the capacity/tax half.** It's the same *family* as what this stack already has: `unsloth-off` (save_on_cpu) and asym's fine-grained offload (`attnact1`, `KEEP_ACTS_HBM`, pinned expact pools) are activation-offload-to-CPU too. Total bytes moved per step don't shrink — and our measured price for full act-offload is unsloth-off's ~57%/token. Megatron's regularity buys better overlap and no allocator churn, not fewer bytes; the b1 OOM walls would move only a few percent.
3. **For the deep end specifically, thrash is nearly moot anyway** — at b1/b2 the memory granularity (30–75 GiB/step) jumps straight from healthy fit to OOM; we measured only mild edge penalties (+0–6%), not real thrash.

So: "easily mediated" = true for thrash-as-allocator-churn (regular pooled offload is the fix, and Megatron's file is a good reference implementation for asym), false for thrash-as-capacity-limit. Meanwhile R21 (asym-lat 600k b1) is still stepping on the GPU.

[2026-07-17T21:13:43.657Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Checked the code — split answer:

**CPU side: yes, pooled.** `asym_gemm/training/activation_offload.py` has a shape-keyed, size-capped, reusable **pinned-CPU buffer pool** (`_CPU_BUFFER_POOL`, evictions + pin-fallback stats) — same idea as Megatron's host side.

**GPU side: no pool.** Reload/staging buffers are fresh `torch.empty`/`empty_strided` per call → they go through the torch caching allocator. That's exactly the Megatron piece we lack (`GPUTensorPool`), and it shows up in our data as the **62 GiB reserve-vs-alloc fragmentation gap** at asym 208k b5.

**Do we have thrashing?** No — nowhere in the c14 deep-end did we hit real thrash (≥1.5× blowup): asym at 97% ran only +1% over linear, superoffload edges were +0–6%. Our near-ceiling disease is different: **fragmentation eats capacity, not speed** — asym reserves ~1.5× what it allocates at high batch, which is what killed b5 (and b6). A Megatron-style GPU pool would recover roughly that 60 GiB of headroom (≈ +1–2 batch at 208k) rather than fix a slowdown. True thrash only exists in c12's ≤64k big-batch superoffload rows.

Grounded in our own measurements — **it buys capacity, not speed:**

- **Speed: ≈nothing.** Asym's tok/s is batch-flat (1883/1867/1864 at b2/b4/b5 @208k) — per-token cost dominates, allocation isn't in the hot path. Only speed win is avoiding the near-ceiling penalty (+1–6% we measured at 95–98%), i.e. tiny.
- **Capacity: big.** The pool would close the reserve-vs-alloc fragmentation gap we measured: 62 GiB wasted at b5, 57 at b4 (asym reserves ~1.5× what it allocates at high B). Recovering that = **+2–3 batch at 208k** (b7–b8 alloc-fits), **b1→b2 at 480k**, and asym-lat's b1 seq-wall stretches roughly from ~950k to ~1.3M+.
- **What that's worth:** since tok/s is batch-flat, extra batch ≠ extra throughput — so the pool strengthens asym's *capacity/max-seq advocacy* (bigger batch than superoffload at every seq, deeper walls), not the tok/s race.
- **Verdict:** beneficial and cheap-ish to add (shapes are stable per layer → good pool fit), but it's the *second* priority: it amplifies the capacity story we're already winning, and does nothing for the −4…−10% per-token gap, which is transfer/compute-bound.

# Git commands
gsync() {
  local branch=$(git branch --show-current)
  local targets=() msg="updates"
  while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    if [ -e "$1" ]; then
      targets+=("$1")
      shift
    else
      msg="$*"
      break
    fi
  done
  [ ${#targets[@]} -eq 0 ] && targets=(".")
  git add "${targets[@]}" &&
  git commit -m "$msg" &&
  git push origin "$branch"
}
gupload() {
  local msg="${*:-updates}" 
  local branch=$(git branch --show-current)
  git commit -m "$msg" &&
  git push origin "$branch"
}
gpull() {
  local branch=$(git branch --show-current)
  git pull origin "$branch"
}
gpush() { git push origin "$(git branch --show-current)"; }
ginit() {
  local url="$1"
  [ -z "$url" ] && { echo "Usage: ginit <url>"; return 1; }
  git init &&
  git add . &&
  git commit -m "first commit" &&
  git branch -M main &&
  git remote add origin "$url" &&
  git push -u origin main
}
gconfig() {
  git config --global user.name "Kevin Ni"
  git config --global user.email "kevinni20020715@gmail.com"
  git config --global credential.helper store
  git config --global --add safe.directory "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
  env -u GIT_ASKPASS -u SSH_ASKPASS GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=1 git pull
}
greset() {
    local branch
    branch="$(git branch --show-current)" || return 1

    if [ -z "$branch" ]; then
        echo "Error: not on a branch, or not inside a git repo"
        return 1
    fi

    echo "WARNING: this will delete ALL local changes, untracked files, and ignored files."
    echo "Resetting current branch '$branch' to origin/$branch"
    read -r -p "Continue? [y/N] " ans

    case "$ans" in
        [yY]|[yY][eE][sS])
            git fetch origin &&
            git reset --hard "origin/$branch" &&
            git clean -fd
            ;;
        *)
            echo "Aborted."
            return 1
            ;;
    esac
}
# gbackup <branch> — back up ALL commits + uncommitted/untracked work to <branch>.
# commit everything on the current branch -> label it <branch> -> reset back one.
# reset --mixed moves the branch pointer only: no file is touched, your changes
# are simply uncommitted again (any partial staging is unstaged). Never pushes.
gbackup() {
  local b="${1:?usage: gbackup <branch>}"
  [ "$b" = "$(git branch --show-current)" ] &&
    { echo "gbackup: refusing: '$b' is the branch you are on — give a backup name" >&2; return 1; }
  git add -A &&
  git commit -q --allow-empty -m "gbackup: $(date '+%F %T')" &&
  git branch -f "$b" HEAD &&
  git reset -q HEAD~1 &&
  echo "gbackup: $b -> $(git rev-parse --short "$b")" &&
  git push -q -f origin "$b" &&
  echo "gbackup: pushed to origin/$b"
}
# Slurm commands
#region ssmi
ssmi() {
  python3 - <<'PY'
import re
import subprocess


def run(cmd):
    return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False).stdout


def parse_gres_total(s):
    m = re.search(r"gpu:(\d+)", s)
    return int(m.group(1)) if m else 0


def idx_to_set(idx_str):
    used = set()
    if not idx_str:
        return used
    for part in idx_str.split(","):
        if "-" in part:
            a, b = part.split("-")
            used.update(range(int(a), int(b) + 1))
        else:
            used.add(int(part))
    return used


nodes = {}
seen = set()
for line in run(["sinfo", "-h", "-N", "-O", "NodeList:25,Gres:35"]).splitlines():
    parts = line.split()
    if len(parts) < 2:
        continue
    name = parts[0]
    if name in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(name)
    nodes[name] = {"total": parse_gres_total(parts[1]), "gpu_user": {}}

job_user = {}
for line in run(["squeue", "-h", "-t", "R", "-o", "%i|%u|%q"]).splitlines():
    try:
        jid, user, qos = line.split("|", 2)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    user = user.strip()
    qos = qos.strip().lower()
    if qos == "scavenger":
        user = f"{user}(s)"
    job_user[jid.strip()] = user

for jid, user in job_user.items():
    out = run(["scontrol", "-d", "show", "job", jid])
    for m in re.finditer(r"Nodes=([\w.\-]+).*?GRES=gpu:\d+\(IDX:([0-9,\-]+)\)", out):
        node, idx_str = m.group(1), m.group(2)
        if node not in nodes:
            continue
        for gpu_idx in idx_to_set(idx_str):
            nodes[node]["gpu_user"][gpu_idx] = user

for name in sorted(nodes):
    info = nodes[name]
    short = name.replace(".ib", "").replace("unites", "U")
    total = info["total"]
    gpu_user = info["gpu_user"]
    used = len(gpu_user)
    free = total - used
    free_ids = sorted(set(range(total)) - set(gpu_user))

    free_str = f"free:{free}" + (f"[{','.join(map(str, free_ids))}]" if free_ids else "")
    gpu_map = " ".join(
        f"{i}:{gpu_user[i]}" if i in gpu_user else f"{i}:-"
        for i in range(total)
    )
    print(f"{short:<4} {name:<14} {used:>2}/{total} {free_str:<18} | {gpu_map}")
PY
}
#endregion ssmi
puser() {
  local pid="$1"
  [ -z "$pid" ] && { echo "Usage: puser <PID>"; return 1; }
  ps -p "$pid" -o user=
}
# Overleaf commands
#region olsetup
olsetup() {
  bash -s -- "$@" <<'__OVERLEAF_EMBEDDED_BASH__'
# overleaf.sh -- prep a freshly-cloned Overleaf project for the local
# Docker-based TL2025 build pipeline (build.sh + texlive-exec.sh + .vscode).
#
# Drops in:
#   - build.sh             one-shot batch build into .build/
#   - texlive-exec.sh      persistent project-scoped TL2025 container for VS Code
#   - .vscode/settings.json LaTeX Workshop wired to texlive-exec.sh
#   - .latexmkrc           guard so plain latexmk still writes into .build/
#   - ancestor .vscode/settings.json wiring when opened from a parent workspace
#   - local exclude entries for build/tooling files
#
# Each project gets its own container name so multiple projects on the same
# machine do not collide.
set -euo pipefail

PROG="olsetup"

usage() {
  cat <<'EOF'
Usage: PROG_PLACEHOLDER [project_path] [options]
       PROG_PLACEHOLDER -d <project_path> [options]
       PROG_PLACEHOLDER -m <main_tex_path> [options]   # uses cwd as project_path

Options:
  -d, --dir <path>     Project directory to set up           (default: $PWD)
  -m, --main <file>    Main .tex file, relative to --dir or absolute
                       (default: infer main.tex or the only \documentclass file)
  -n, --name <suffix>  Container name suffix                 (default: basename of dir)
  -i, --image <image>  TeX Live image                        (default: texlive/texlive:TL2025-historic)
  -f, --force          Overwrite existing build files
      --no-pull        Skip Docker image prefetch
  -w, --watch          After setup, run ./build.sh --watch (blocking, live rebuild)
  -h, --help           Show this help

Examples:
  PROG_PLACEHOLDER .                                # infer main in cwd
  PROG_PLACEHOLDER ~/papers/foo                     # infer main in given dir
  PROG_PLACEHOLDER -d ~/papers/foo -m main.tex      # explicit root main
  PROG_PLACEHOLDER -d ~/papers/foo -m latex/paper.tex # explicit subdir main
  PROG_PLACEHOLDER -m paper.tex -n foo --watch      # custom container + live rebuild
EOF
}

DIR="$PWD"
MAIN=""
NAME=""
IMAGE="texlive/texlive:TL2025-historic"
FORCE=0
PULL=1
WATCH=0
POSITIONAL_DIR_SEEN=0

while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  case "$1" in
    -d|--dir)
      [[ $# -ge 2 ]] || { echo "Missing value for $1" >&2; usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2; exit 1; }
      DIR="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    -m|--main)
      [[ $# -ge 2 ]] || { echo "Missing value for $1" >&2; usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2; exit 1; }
      MAIN="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    -n|--name)
      [[ $# -ge 2 ]] || { echo "Missing value for $1" >&2; usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2; exit 1; }
      NAME="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    -i|--image)
      [[ $# -ge 2 ]] || { echo "Missing value for $1" >&2; usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2; exit 1; }
      IMAGE="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    -f|--force) FORCE=1; shift ;;
    --no-pull)  PULL=0; shift ;;
    -w|--watch) WATCH=1; shift ;;
    -h|--help)  usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g"; exit 0 ;;
    --) shift; break ;;
    -*)
      echo "Unknown option: $1" >&2
      usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2
      exit 1 ;;
    *)
      if [[ $POSITIONAL_DIR_SEEN -eq 1 ]]; then
        echo "Unexpected argument: $1" >&2
        usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2
        exit 1
      fi
      DIR="$1"
      POSITIONAL_DIR_SEEN=1
      shift ;;
  esac
done
if [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; then
  if [[ $POSITIONAL_DIR_SEEN -eq 0 && $# -eq 1 ]]; then
    DIR="$1"
  else
    echo "Unexpected argument: $1" >&2
    usage | sed "s/PROG_PLACEHOLDER/$PROG/g" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi

# ---- resolve dir ----
[[ -d "$DIR" ]] || { echo "Not a directory: $DIR" >&2; exit 1; }
DIR="$(cd "$DIR" && pwd)"

detect_main_tex() {
  local rel file
  local candidates=()

  if [[ -f "$DIR/main.tex" ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "main.tex"
    return 0
  fi

  while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    rel="${file#"$DIR"/}"
    case "$rel" in
      .build/*|.git/*|agent/*|bak/*|baks/*|backup/*|backups/*)
        continue ;;
    esac
    if grep -Eq '^[[:space:]]*\\document(class|style)([[:space:]]|\[|\{)' "$file"; then
      candidates+=("$rel")
    fi
  done < <(find "$DIR" -type f -name '*.tex' -print0 | sort -z)

  if (( ${#candidates[@]} == 1 )); then
    printf '%s\n' "${candidates[0]}"
    return 0
  fi

  if (( ${#candidates[@]} == 0 )); then
    echo "Could not infer main .tex file in: $DIR" >&2
    echo "Pass --main <main.tex relative to --dir>." >&2
  else
    echo "Could not infer main .tex file because multiple files contain \\documentclass:" >&2
    printf '  %s\n' "${candidates[@]}" >&2
    echo "Pass --main <one of these>." >&2
  fi
  return 1
}

normalize_main_tex() {
  local raw="$1"
  local main_abs

  if [[ "$raw" == /* ]]; then
    [[ -f "$raw" ]] || { echo "Main file not found: $raw" >&2; exit 1; }
    main_abs="$(cd "$(dirname "$raw")" && pwd)/$(basename "$raw")"
  else
    [[ -f "$DIR/$raw" ]] || { echo "Main file not found: $DIR/$raw" >&2; exit 1; }
    main_abs="$(cd "$DIR/$(dirname "$raw")" && pwd)/$(basename "$raw")"
  fi

  case "$main_abs" in
    "$DIR"/*) MAIN="${main_abs#"$DIR"/}" ;;
    *) echo "Main file must be inside project dir: $main_abs" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
}

# ---- container name ----
if [[ -z "$NAME" ]]; then
  NAME="$(basename "$DIR" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -c 'a-z0-9-' '-' | sed 's/-\+/-/g; s/^-//; s/-$//')"
  [[ -n "$NAME" ]] || NAME="proj"
fi
CONTAINER="overleaf-${NAME}"

# ---- main .tex ----
MAIN_INFERRED=0
if [[ -z "$MAIN" ]]; then
  MAIN="$(detect_main_tex)"
  MAIN_INFERRED=1
fi
normalize_main_tex "$MAIN"

# ---- docker sanity ----
if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "docker not found in PATH." >&2; exit 1
fi
if ! docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "docker is installed but not usable by $(id -un). Add user to 'docker' group or run with sudo." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Setting up Overleaf-parity build pipeline:"
echo "  dir       = $DIR"
if [[ $MAIN_INFERRED -eq 1 ]]; then
  echo "  main      = $MAIN (inferred)"
else
  echo "  main      = $MAIN"
fi
echo "  container = $CONTAINER"
echo "  image     = $IMAGE"
echo "  force     = $FORCE"

# ---- helper: write file from stdin, honoring --force ----
write_file() {
  local path="$1" mode="$2"
  if [[ -e "$path" && $FORCE -ne 1 ]]; then
    echo "  skip (exists): ${path#"$DIR"/}  -- use -f to overwrite"
    cat >/dev/null   # drain stdin so heredoc doesn't leak
    return 0
  fi
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$path")"
  cat > "$path"
  chmod "$mode" "$path"
  echo "  wrote: ${path#"$DIR"/}"
}

# Generated pipeline files should self-heal when this setup command is rerun.
# They are local-only and excluded from git/Overleaf sync below.
write_generated_file() {
  local path="$1" mode="$2" action="wrote"
  [[ -e "$path" ]] && action="updated"
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$path")"
  cat > "$path"
  chmod "$mode" "$path"
  echo "  $action: ${path#"$DIR"/}"
}

# ---- build.sh (one-shot) ----
write_generated_file "$DIR/build.sh" 755 <<EOF
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build $MAIN using the same TeX Live as Overleaf (TL2025, pdfLaTeX).
# Output -> .build/
set -euo pipefail

cd "\$(dirname "\$(readlink -f "\$0")")"
mkdir -p .build

export GOMAXPROCS="\${GOMAXPROCS:-2}"

IMAGE="$IMAGE"
MAIN="\${1:-$MAIN}"

EXTRA=()
if [[ "\${1:-}" == "--watch" || "\${2:-}" == "--watch" ]]; then
  EXTRA+=(-pvc -view=none)
  MAIN="\${MAIN/--watch/}"
  MAIN="\${MAIN:-$MAIN}"
fi

docker run --rm -t \\
  -v "\$PWD:/work" \\
  -w /work \\
  -u "\$(id -u):\$(id -g)" \\
  "\$IMAGE" \\
  latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \\
          -output-directory=.build "\${EXTRA[@]}" "\$MAIN"
EOF

# ---- .latexmkrc (guard for plain latexmk invocations) ----
# When --main lives in a subdir, kpathsea won't find sty/bib/bst files that
# sit alongside it (e.g. acl.sty, custom.bib, acl_natbib.bst) because cwd is
# the project root. Add the main file's directory to the search paths so
# `\usepackage{...}` / `\bibliography{...}` / `\bibliographystyle{...}` work
# regardless of where the main file lives in the project tree.
EXTRA_LATEXMKRC=""
if [[ "$MAIN" == */* ]]; then
  MAIN_DIR="${MAIN%/*}"
  EXTRA_LATEXMKRC=$'\n'"ensure_path('TEXINPUTS', './$MAIN_DIR');
ensure_path('BIBINPUTS', './$MAIN_DIR');
ensure_path('BSTINPUTS', './$MAIN_DIR');"
fi
LATEXMKRC_BLOCK=$(cat <<EOF
# >>> overleaf.sh managed block >>>
# Local guard: keep latexmk artifacts out of the Overleaf project root.
# This applies even when someone runs plain \`latexmk main.tex\` instead of
# the generated ./build.sh or VS Code recipe.
\$out_dir = '.build';
\$aux_dir = '.build';
$EXTRA_LATEXMKRC
# <<< overleaf.sh managed block <<<
EOF
)
if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  OVERLEAF_LATEXMKRC_BLOCK="$LATEXMKRC_BLOCK" python3 - "$DIR/.latexmkrc" <<'PY'
import os
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(sys.argv[1])
block = os.environ["OVERLEAF_LATEXMKRC_BLOCK"].rstrip() + "\n"
begin = "# >>> overleaf.sh managed block >>>"
end = "# <<< overleaf.sh managed block <<<"
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
if path.exists():
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    pattern = re.compile(
        re.escape(begin) + r".*?" + re.escape(end) + r"\n?",
        re.DOTALL,
    )
    legacy = re.compile(
        r"\A# Local guard: keep latexmk artifacts out of the Overleaf project root\.\n"
        r"# This applies even when someone runs plain `latexmk main\.tex` instead of\n"
        r"# the generated \./build\.sh or VS Code recipe\.\n"
        r"\$out_dir = '\.build';\n"
        r"\$aux_dir = '\.build';\n"
        r"(?:ensure_path\('[A-Z]+INPUTS', '\./[^']+'\);\n)*\n*",
        re.DOTALL,
    )
    if pattern.search(text):
        text = pattern.sub(block, text)
        text = legacy.sub("", text)
    else:
        text = legacy.sub("", text).strip()
        text = (text + "\n\n" if text else "") + block
else:
    text = block
path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
print(f"  updated: {path.name}")
PY
  chmod 644 "$DIR/.latexmkrc"
else
  write_file "$DIR/.latexmkrc" 644 <<EOF
$LATEXMKRC_BLOCK
EOF
fi

# ---- texlive-exec.sh (persistent container for LaTeX Workshop) ----
write_generated_file "$DIR/texlive-exec.sh" 755 <<EOF
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run latexmk inside a persistent TL2025 container (Overleaf parity).
# Project-scoped container: $CONTAINER
# Mounts the project at the same absolute path inside and outside the container
# so SyncTeX / VS Code "jump to so" resolve transparently.
set -euo pipefail

export GOMAXPROCS="\${GOMAXPROCS:-2}"

CONTAINER="$CONTAINER"
IMAGE="$IMAGE"
PROJECT_DIR="\$(cd "\$(dirname "\$(readlink -f "\$0")")" && pwd)"

if ! docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -q "^\${CONTAINER}\$"; then
  docker rm -f "\$CONTAINER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  docker run -d \\
    --name "\$CONTAINER" \\
    --restart unless-stopped \\
    -v "\$PROJECT_DIR:\$PROJECT_DIR" \\
    -w "\$PROJECT_DIR" \\
    -u "\$(id -u):\$(id -g)" \\
    --entrypoint "" \\
    "\$IMAGE" \\
    sleep infinity >/dev/null
fi

exec docker exec -i \\
  -w "\$PROJECT_DIR" \\
  "\$CONTAINER" \\
  latexmk "\$@"
EOF

# ---- .vscode/settings.json (LaTeX Workshop wiring) ----
PROJECT_SETTINGS="$DIR/.vscode/settings.json"
if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  python3 - "$PROJECT_SETTINGS" <<'PY'
import json
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(sys.argv[1])
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
try:
    data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") or "{}") if path.exists() else {}
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    backup = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".bak")
    shutil.copy2(path, backup)
    print(f"  backed up non-strict JSON settings: {backup}")
    data = {}
if not isinstance(data, dict):
    data = {}

recipe_name = "latexmk (TL2025 / Overleaf parity)"
tool_name = "latexmk"
data["latex-workshop.docker.enabled"] = False
data["latex-workshop.linting.chktex.enabled"] = False
data["latex-workshop.linting.lacheck.enabled"] = False
data["latex-workshop.latex.outDir"] = ".build"
data["latex-workshop.latex.autoBuild.run"] = "onSave"
data["latex-workshop.latex.autoClean.run"] = "never"
data["latex-workshop.latex.recipe.default"] = recipe_name
data["latex-workshop.view.pdf.viewer"] = "tab"
data["latex-workshop.view.pdf.invertMode.enabled"] = "never"

recipe = {"name": recipe_name, "tools": [tool_name]}
tool = {
    "name": tool_name,
    "command": "./texlive-exec.sh",
    "args": [
        "-pdf",
        "-interaction=nonstopmode",
        "-synctex=1",
        "-file-line-error",
        "-halt-on-error",
        "-outdir=%OUTDIR%",
        "%DOC%",
    ],
    "env": {},
}

recipes = data.get("latex-workshop.latex.recipes", [])
if not isinstance(recipes, list):
    recipes = []
recipes = [r for r in recipes if not (isinstance(r, dict) and r.get("name") == recipe_name)]
data["latex-workshop.latex.recipes"] = [recipe] + recipes

tools = data.get("latex-workshop.latex.tools", [])
if not isinstance(tools, list):
    tools = []
tools = [t for t in tools if not (isinstance(t, dict) and t.get("name") == tool_name)]
data["latex-workshop.latex.tools"] = [tool] + tools

associations = data.get("files.associations", {})
if not isinstance(associations, dict):
    associations = {}
associations["*.tex"] = "latex"
data["files.associations"] = associations

path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(f"  updated: {path.relative_to(path.parents[1])}")
PY
  chmod 644 "$PROJECT_SETTINGS"
else
  write_file "$PROJECT_SETTINGS" 644 <<'EOF'
{
  "latex-workshop.docker.enabled": false,
  "latex-workshop.linting.chktex.enabled": false,
  "latex-workshop.linting.lacheck.enabled": false,

  "latex-workshop.latex.autoBuild.run": "onSave",
  "latex-workshop.latex.autoClean.run": "never",

  "latex-workshop.view.pdf.viewer": "tab",

# ---- parent workspace settings (when VS Code is opened above this project) ----
# VS Code ignores nested .vscode/settings.json if the user opened a parent repo
# as the workspace. Merge a generic project-local LaTeX Workshop recipe into
# useful ancestor workspaces:
#   - the immediate parent directory of the Overleaf repo
#   - every existing ancestor .vscode/settings.json
#   - the first outer git repository root above the Overleaf repo
#
# That covers opening the project itself, a directory that groups Overleaf repos,
# or the larger code repo that contains them without creating settings in every
# intermediate directory.
WORKSPACE_SETTINGS=()
add_workspace_settings() {
  local path="$1" create="$2" existing
  for existing in "${WORKSPACE_SETTINGS[@]}"; do
    [[ "$existing" == "$path" ]] && return 0
  done
  if [[ "$create" == "1" ]]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$path")"
    if [[ ! -e "$path" ]]; then
      printf '{}\n' > "$path"
      echo "  created parent workspace settings: $path"
    fi
  fi
  if [[ -f "$path" ]]; then
    WORKSPACE_SETTINGS+=("$path")
  fi
  return 0
}

add_workspace_settings "$(dirname "$DIR")/.vscode/settings.json" 1

SEARCH_DIR="$(dirname "$DIR")"
while [[ "$SEARCH_DIR" != "/" && -n "$SEARCH_DIR" ]]; do
  add_workspace_settings "$SEARCH_DIR/.vscode/settings.json" 0
  SEARCH_DIR="$(dirname "$SEARCH_DIR")"
done

OUTER_GIT_ROOT=""
SEARCH_DIR="$(dirname "$DIR")"
while [[ "$SEARCH_DIR" != "/" && -n "$SEARCH_DIR" ]]; do
  if [[ -e "$SEARCH_DIR/.git" ]]; then
    OUTER_GIT_ROOT="$SEARCH_DIR"
    break
  fi
  SEARCH_DIR="$(dirname "$SEARCH_DIR")"
done

if [[ -n "$OUTER_GIT_ROOT" ]]; then
  add_workspace_settings "$OUTER_GIT_ROOT/.vscode/settings.json" 1
fi

if (( ${#WORKSPACE_SETTINGS[@]} > 0 )); then
  if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    python3 - "${WORKSPACE_SETTINGS[@]}" <<'PY'
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

recipe_name = "latexmk (project-local Overleaf parity)"
tool_name = "latexmk-project-local"
for arg in sys.argv[1:]:
    path = Path(arg)
    try:
        data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") or "{}")
    except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
        print(f"  skip parent workspace settings (not strict JSON): {path} ({exc})")
        continue

    data["latex-workshop.docker.enabled"] = False
    data["latex-workshop.linting.chktex.enabled"] = False
    data["latex-workshop.linting.lacheck.enabled"] = False
    data["latex-workshop.latex.outDir"] = "%DIR%/.build"
    data["latex-workshop.latex.autoBuild.run"] = "onSave"
    data["latex-workshop.latex.autoClean.run"] = "never"
    data["latex-workshop.latex.recipe.default"] = recipe_name
    data["latex-workshop.view.pdf.viewer"] = "tab"
    data["latex-workshop.view.pdf.invertMode.enabled"] = "never"

    recipe = {"name": recipe_name, "tools": [tool_name]}
    tool = {
        "name": tool_name,
        "command": "/bin/bash",
        "args": [
            "-lc",
            "cd \"%DIR%\" && ./texlive-exec.sh -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode "
            "-synctex=1 -file-line-error -halt-on-error "
            "-outdir=\"%OUTDIR%\" \"%DOC%\"",
        ],
        "env": {},
    }

    recipes = data.get("latex-workshop.latex.recipes", [])
    if not isinstance(recipes, list):
        recipes = []
    recipes = [r for r in recipes if not (isinstance(r, dict) and r.get("name") == recipe_name)]
    data["latex-workshop.latex.recipes"] = [recipe] + recipes

    tools = data.get("latex-workshop.latex.tools", [])
    if not isinstance(tools, list):
        tools = []
    tools = [t for t in tools if not (isinstance(t, dict) and t.get("name") == tool_name)]
    data["latex-workshop.latex.tools"] = [tool] + tools

    path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"  updated parent workspace settings: {path}")
PY
  else
    echo "  skip parent workspace settings: python3 not found"
  fi

  # These parent settings are local editor plumbing. Keep them out of the
  # containing code repo's status when they live inside a git checkout.
  for settings in "${WORKSPACE_SETTINGS[@]}"; do
    workspace_dir="$(dirname "$(dirname "$settings")")"
    if git -C "$workspace_dir" rev-parse --show-toplevel >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      top="$(git -C "$workspace_dir" rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
      common="$(git -C "$workspace_dir" rev-parse --git-common-dir)"
      case "$common" in
        /*) ;;
        *) common="$top/$common" ;;
      esac
      case "$settings" in
        "$top"/*) rel="${settings#"$top"/}" ;;
        *) continue ;;
      esac
      mkdir -p "$common/info"
      touch "$common/info/exclude"
      if ! grep -Fxq "$rel" "$common/info/exclude"; then
        printf '%s\n' "$rel" >> "$common/info/exclude"
        echo "  added to parent git exclude: $rel"
      fi
    fi
  done
fi

# ---- exclude pipeline files locally so they don't push back to Overleaf ----
# Prefer .git/info/exclude (per-clone, untracked, never pushed). This matches
# the existing convention in the bootstrap project. Outside a git repo, fall
# back to .gitignore.
EXCLUDE_PATTERNS=(
  ".build/"
  "agent/"
  "build.sh"
  "texlive-exec.sh"
  ".vscode/"
  ".latexmkrc"
  "*.aux"
  "*.log"
  "*.out"
  "*.fls"
  "*.fdb_latexmk"
  "*.bbl"
  "*.blg"
  "*.synctex.gz"
)

if git -C "$DIR" rev-parse --git-common-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  COMMON="$(git -C "$DIR" rev-parse --git-common-dir)"
  case "$COMMON" in
    /*) ;;
    *)  COMMON="$DIR/$COMMON" ;;
  esac
  EXFILE="$COMMON/info/exclude"
  TARGET_LABEL=".git/info/exclude (local-only, not pushed)"
else
  EXFILE="$DIR/.gitignore"
  TARGET_LABEL=".gitignore (tracked)"
fi
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$EXFILE")"
touch "$EXFILE"

added=()
for pat in "${EXCLUDE_PATTERNS[@]}"; do
  if ! grep -Fxq "$pat" "$EXFILE"; then
    printf '%s\n' "$pat" >> "$EXFILE"
    added+=("$pat")
  fi
done
if (( ${#added[@]} > 0 )); then
  echo "  added to $TARGET_LABEL: ${added[*]}"
else
  echo "  $TARGET_LABEL already excludes pipeline files"
fi

# ---- remove stale root-level artifacts ----
# These are generated by accidental plain latexmk/pdflatex runs. All build
# output should live in .build/. Sweep every untracked file in the project
# root whose extension is a known LaTeX/BibTeX artifact, regardless of stem,
# so per-file aux output (e.g. checklist.aux, sections/foo.aux) is also
# cleaned. Tracked files are always preserved.
MAIN_STEM="${MAIN%.tex}"
ARTIFACT_EXTS=(
  aux bbl blg bcf fdb_latexmk fls log out toc lof lot
  nav snm vrb idx ind ilg glo gls glg acn acr alg
  synctex.gz synctex run.xml dvi ps
)
in_git=0
if git -C "$DIR" rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  in_git=1
fi
is_tracked() {
  local rel="$1"
  (( in_git )) || return 1
  git -C "$DIR" ls-files --error-unmatch -- "$rel" >/dev/null 2>&1
}
removed=()
kept=()
shopt -s nullglob
for ext in "${ARTIFACT_EXTS[@]}"; do
  for path in "$DIR"/*."$ext"; do
    [[ -f "$path" ]] || continue
    rel="${path#"$DIR"/}"
    if is_tracked "$rel"; then
      kept+=("$rel")
      continue
    fi
    rm -f "$path"
    removed+=("$rel")
  done
done
# Main-file PDF: only remove if untracked (some projects commit a built PDF).
if [[ -f "$DIR/$MAIN_STEM.pdf" ]]; then
  if is_tracked "$MAIN_STEM.pdf"; then
    kept+=("$MAIN_STEM.pdf")
  else
    rm -f "$DIR/$MAIN_STEM.pdf"
    removed+=("$MAIN_STEM.pdf")
  fi
fi
shopt -u nullglob
for k in "${kept[@]}"; do
  echo "  keep tracked root artifact: $k"
done
if (( ${#removed[@]} > 0 )); then
  echo "  removed stale root artifacts: ${removed[*]}"
fi

# ---- prefetch image ----
if [[ $PULL -eq 1 ]]; then
  if ! docker image inspect "$IMAGE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "Pulling $IMAGE (one-time, large)..."
    docker pull "$IMAGE"
  else
    echo "  image already present: $IMAGE"
  fi
fi

cat <<EOF

Done.
  Build once:    cd "$DIR" && ./build.sh
  Watch mode:    cd "$DIR" && ./build.sh --watch
  VS Code:       open "$DIR" -- LaTeX Workshop will use texlive-exec.sh on save.

Container will be created on first build as: $CONTAINER
Stop it later with:  docker rm -f $CONTAINER
EOF

if [[ $WATCH -eq 1 ]]; then
  echo
  echo "Starting live rebuild (Ctrl-C to stop)..."
  cd "$DIR"
  exec ./build.sh --watch
fi
__OVERLEAF_EMBEDDED_BASH__
}
#endregion olsetup
olclone() {
  if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: olclone PROJECT_ID" >&2
    return 2
  fi

  if [ -z "${OVERLEAF_KEY:-}" ]; then
    echo "olclone: OVERLEAF_KEY is not set" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  local project_id="$1"
  git clone "https://git:${OVERLEAF_KEY}@git.overleaf.com/${project_id}"
}
# Orthrus commands
auth_orthrus() {
  kinit
  ORTHRUS_REGION=I18N-OG orthrus-cli demand fdbd:dc62:3:302::14 -t 24
  ORTHRUS_REGION=I18N-OG orthrus-cli demand fdbd:dc62:3:302::15 -t 24
}
# Tunnel commands
tunnel_start() {
  local name="$1"
  if [ -z "$name" ]; then echo "usage: tunnel_start <name>"; return 1; fi

  local dir="$TUNNEL_DIR/$name"
  mkdir -p "$dir"/{logs,server-data,extensions,cli-data}

  nohup "$CODE_BIN" --cli-data-dir "$dir/cli-data" tunnel \
      --accept-server-license-terms \
      --name "$name" \
      --server-data-dir "$dir/server-data" \
      --extensions-dir "$dir/extensions" \
      > "$dir/logs/tunnel.log" 2>&1 &

  echo "tunnel '$name' starting — log: $dir/logs/tunnel.log"
}
tunnel_crontab() {
  local name="$1"
  if [ -z "$name" ]; then echo "usage: tunnel_crontab <name>"; return 1; fi

  if crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -Fq "tunnel_start $name"; then
      echo "tunnel '$name' already registered in crontab"
      return 0
  fi

  (crontab -l 2>/dev/null; \
    echo "@reboot sleep 30 && /bin/bash -lc 'source \"\$HOME/env/bashrc.sh\"; tunnel_start $name'") | crontab -
  echo "registered '$name' for reboot via crontab"
}

# Rsync aliases
alias rsyncd='rsync -aHAX --delete --info=progress2 --partial'
# Tmux aliases
tmux() { command tmux -S "$CUSTOM_TMUX_SOCK" "$@"; }
tsend() {
  if [[ $# -lt 2 || -z "$1" ]]; then
    echo "usage: tsend <session[:window[.pane]]> \"<command>\"" >&2
    echo "example: tsend kevin \"bash a.sh; bash b.sh\"" >&2
    return 2
  fi

  if [[ $# -gt 2 ]]; then
    echo "tsend: command must be passed as one quoted argument." >&2
    echo "wrong:   tsend kevin bash a.sh; bash b.sh" >&2
    echo "correct: tsend kevin \"bash a.sh; bash b.sh\"" >&2
    return 2
  fi

  local target="$1"
  local cmd="$2"
  local session="${target%%:*}"
  local sock="${TSEND_TMUX_SOCKET:-$CUSTOM_TMUX_SOCK}"

  if [[ -z "$cmd" ]]; then
    echo "tsend: empty command" >&2
    return 2
  fi

  if ! command tmux -S "$sock" has-session -t "$session" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "tsend: tmux session not found: $session on socket $sock" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  command tmux -S "$sock" send-keys -t "$target" -l -- "$cmd"
  command tmux -S "$sock" send-keys -t "$target" C-m
}
tkill() {
  local s
  for s in "$@"; do
    tmux kill-session -t "$s"
  done
}
alias tnew="tmux new -A -s"
alias tatt="tmux attach -t"
alias trename="tmux rename-session -t"
alias tls="tmux ls"
# Process aliases
alias term="kill -TERM"
alias int="kill -INT"

# Engine. Args: <name> <host-persistent-folder>
# Mounts <host-persistent-folder> -> /workspace/<folder-name> (workdir).
# Always auto-mounts custom env as /workspace/env.
# Runs setup.sh on first creation OR if claude is missing.
_custom_enroot_run() {
  local name="$1"
  local host_folder="$2"
  shift 2

  local workdir="/workspace/$(basename "${host_folder}")"
  local gpus=""

  for arg in "$@"; do
    case "${arg}" in
      --gpus=*)
        gpus="${arg#--gpus=}"
        ;;
      *)
        echo "[custom-enroot] unknown argument: ${arg}" >&2
        return 2
        ;;
    esac
  done

  _custom_enroot_prepare
  mkdir -p "${host_folder}" "${CUSTOM_ENROOT_CACHE}"

  local _first_run=false
  if ! _custom_enroot_exec enroot list | grep -qx "${name}"; then
    _custom_enroot_exec enroot create --name "${name}" "${CUSTOM_ENROOT_DEFAULT_IMAGE}"
    _first_run=true
  fi

  # Pre-create mount targets in the rootfs (enroot 3.x requirement).
  local rootfs="${CUSTOM_ENROOT_DATA_PATH}/${name}"
  mkdir -p "${rootfs}${workdir}" "${rootfs}/workspace/env" 2>/dev/null || true

  # Ensure container shells source shared env-setup script.
  # Also strip stale source lines from old layouts baked into the base image.
  local env_source_line='source /workspace/env/bashrc.sh'
  local target
  for target in "${rootfs}/root/.bashrc" "${rootfs}/home/$(id -un)/.bashrc"; do
    if [[ -f "$target" ]]; then
      sed -i '/source \/workspace\/AsymGEMM-SFT/d' "$target"
      grep -qxF "$env_source_line" "$target" || printf '\n%s\n' "$env_source_line" >> "$target"
    fi
  done

  local mounts=(
    "--mount=${host_folder}:${workdir}"
    "--mount=${CUSTOM_ENROOT_WS}/env:/workspace/env:rw,bind"
    "--mount=${CUSTOM_ENROOT_CACHE}:${CUSTOM_ENROOT_CACHE}"
  )

  local envs=()
  if [[ -n "${gpus}" ]]; then
    envs=(
      --env "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${gpus}"
      --env "NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${gpus}"
    )
  fi

  local _need_setup=false
  local _setup_reason=""

  if [[ "$_first_run" == true ]]; then
    _need_setup=true
    _setup_reason="new container"
  # NOTE: claude installs as a symlink to an absolute in-container path, so from
  # the host `-x`/`-e` would follow it to the host root and read as missing. Use
  # `-L` (symlink exists) / `-d` (install dir) so the check is host-side correct.
  elif [[ ! -e "${rootfs}/usr/local/bin/claude" && ! -L "${rootfs}/usr/local/bin/claude" &&
          ! -e "${rootfs}/root/.local/bin/claude" && ! -L "${rootfs}/root/.local/bin/claude" &&
          ! -d "${rootfs}/root/.local/share/claude" ]]; then
    _need_setup=true
    _setup_reason="claude missing"
  fi

  if [[ "$_need_setup" == true ]]; then
    echo "[custom-enroot] Setup for '${name}' (${_setup_reason}) — installing node, codex, claude-code..."
    _custom_enroot_exec enroot start --rw --root "${mounts[@]}" "${envs[@]}" "${name}" \
      /bin/bash -c "bash /workspace/env/setup.sh --proxy no" \
      && echo "[custom-enroot] Setup complete." \
      || echo "[custom-enroot] WARNING: setup failed — some tools may be missing."
  fi

  _custom_enroot_exec enroot start --rw --root "${mounts[@]}" "${envs[@]}" "${name}" \
    /bin/bash -lc "cd '${workdir}' && exec bash -i"
}
custom_enroot_status() {
  _custom_enroot_prepare

  printf "CUSTOM_ENROOT_WS=%s\nCUSTOM_ENROOT_DATA_PATH=%s\n" \
    "${CUSTOM_ENROOT_WS}" "${CUSTOM_ENROOT_DATA_PATH}"

  _custom_enroot_exec enroot list
}

**`scheduler_v2.md` now carries §8 — the full-range scheduler, v3.** The meticulous commentary, structured as you asked:

**What the formal system is.** One procedure: enumerate (backend-family × batch) candidates → **health filter** (capacity model + the measured allocator-bend; >98% HBM is never emitted, 92–98% carries the measured 0–6% edge penalty) → **throughput model** (per-token cost τ_f(s) with a shared attention term + family tax, and the **knee law**: tok/s is batch-flat beyond ~0.4M tokens/step — the single most load-bearing measurement of the whole campaign) → argmax tok/s, β-tiebreak on memory → asym candidates then nest the existing §4 knob-admission dial. Every emission carries its predicted (M̂, t̂); any probe that disagrees re-fits that family's coefficients. **The regime table is a report the procedure generates, never an input** — that's the "no if-else" property you demanded, made structural.

**How it meets each of your goals, with receipts:**
1. **Complete fallback** — a theorem, not a branch: wherever sup-unsloth's t̂ is argmax (today: the 160–600k batch-flat window, because of the measured +143 us/tok asym backward tax), the scheduler *emits the byte-identical superoffload config* — baseline preserved by construction.
2. **Thrashing settings → larger batch**: the health filter auto-rejects every measured thrash/edge-dominated row (sup 16k b40 ×1.6, 320k b2-edge 1355<1436 — never emitted), and below the knee asym's leaner per-sample admits the batch sup couldn't hold: measured +23% over sup at 120k×8, +6% at 80k×8, strict domination of sup-unsloth-off everywhere.
3. **Fast mode**: emerges at s ≲ 130k — and it's *faster than the baselines there*, not merely equal (so the fallback instinct was right in spirit, and the data says asym-L3 already is the fast mode).
4. **Ultimate memory mode**: emerges past the measured walls (F1 dead >660k) with zero mode-specific logic — 800k @ 597 tok/s is just the argmax over the only feasible family.

**The one honest gap, and the lever:** today's middle window belongs to superoffload only because of the +143 us/tok backward tax that `fix_asym.md` has now fully attributed (S0 done: +120 memcpy serial/pageable + 23 wrapper + 23 GEMM) — and §8.4 ranks **S-mem** (kill the 333 GB/step never-read U-offloads, fix pin-fallback, overlap) as the #1 frontier motion: when it lands, the middle window re-prices to asym *automatically, with no scheduler edit*. That is the design's proof of correctness.

**2. The two modes, fully but briefly** — same backend (frozen weights on host, CPU-AdamW LoRA, fg MLP path); they differ on **three switches**:

| switch | asym-lat | asym-mem |
|---|---|---|
| **GEMM engine** | `staged` — stage the weight panel H2D, run *native* cuBLAS (fast) | `asym` kernel — compute straight from pinned-CPU weights (no staging HBM, ~⅓ native speed) |
| **route tensors** | ker000 — materializes route-space [R,H] buffers (HBM cost) | ker101 fused route kernels — never materializes them (HBM saved) |
| **activation residency** | keep-acts: fg acts + attention U/S + GC saves stay in HBM across each layer's fwd→bwd (no CPU round-trips → fast backward) | everything offloaded to CPU per layer (+ ohbm16 roots) → round-trips → slower backward |

Consequence: **lat spends HBM-per-token to buy time; mem spends time to buy capacity.** Both costs scale with tokens in flight — hence the 80 GiB gap at 120k×8 (352.5 s @180 GiB vs 483.6 s @100.3) but only ~5 GiB at small-token anchors, and hence mem's real crown: the leanest per-sample slope → deepest ceilings (b8@174k vs unsloth's 80k). The scheduler's dial moves between them rung-by-rung (balanced = staged only, in the middle), and in the deep-end b1 regime the levers are nearly free memory-wise, so it correctly always chose lat.

[2026-07-19T07:28:46.473Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**1. ker000 vs ker101** (measured @120k×8): with the fast GEMM engine, **ker000 is faster: −32.5 s/step — but costs +36 GiB**. ker101 is the reverse: slower, but avoids materializing the big routing buffers, so it's the lean choice. (ker101's custom kernels also only work with the slow streamed engine, which is why the fast mode pairs with ker000.)

**2. Activation residency, plain words:** during training, each layer's forward pass produces big intermediate results that the backward pass needs again later.
- **Latency mode: just leave them in GPU memory** until backward uses them. Costs GPU memory; zero extra work.
- **Memory mode: copy them out to CPU RAM right after forward** (freeing GPU memory), then **copy them back in** when backward needs them. Saves GPU memory; but every layer pays two large copies and the GPU frequently waits on them — that's the slowdown.

That's the whole idea. (My 5 fixes were cases where latency mode was *still* doing some of those copies for no benefit — we deleted them.)

**3. Yes — those three switches are the entire difference**: which GEMM engine, ker000 vs ker101, and keep-vs-copy for the intermediates (memory mode also parks the checkpoint anchors in CPU RAM — same keep-vs-copy idea applied to one more tensor family). Everything else — optimizer on CPU, weight streaming, chunk sizes, loss kernel, LoRA placement — is **identical in both modes**, on purpose: those settings measured as best-for-both and are never dialed.

[2026-07-19T11:19:49.984Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**Answer: No, it's not too hard — it's one formula with one continuous knob, and the campaign data already validates it.** Written up as `scheduler_v2.md` **§9** (v3.1). The essence:

**The one formula** (config x = family × batch × knob-set):

```
x*(model, s; β) = argmax_x   tok/s_x(s,B) − β·M_x(s,B)     s.t. M_x ≤ (1−h)·C
τ_x(s) = a_x + b·s  (per-token cost: family tax + shared attention slope)
M_x(s,B) = base_x + B·m_x·s  (affine capacity)
```

**β is the dial** — tok/s you'll sacrifice per GiB retained. β→0 = pure latency profile, β→∞ = pure memory profile, continuous in between. Inside asym, the *same* β runs against the measured knob ladder (staged ρ=9.2 → ker000 0.90 → keep-acts 0.87 s/GiB): admit knobs while ρ ≥ β and fit holds. Since every knob's memory cost scales with tokens, **at fixed β the admitted set shrinks automatically as s grows: lat → balanced → mem, with no mode enum and no if-else** — "mode" is just where the ladder truncates.

**The constants are measured, and the formula predicts reality** (I refit them from the c14 rows tonight):

| family | τ(s) us/tok | M(s,1) GiB | wall predicted → measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| asym-lat | 126 + 1.94·s | 4.3 + 0.179·s | 987k → 800k healthy ✓ |
| sup-uns | −63 + 2.24·s | 19.9 + 0.253·s | **638k → (640k,660k] ✓** |
| sup-rc | 62 + 2.00·s | 4.1 + 0.452·s | **391k → (392k,400k] ✓** |
| asym-mem | ~3× lat tax | ~5 + 0.119·s | **1477k** (the ultra-long headline) |

**Your desideratum is the default output** (β≈1–3): mid-seqs → sup is argmax = parity by construction; parity onset s_par emerges where the tax dilutes below noise (measured: exactly 600–640k, and every asym fix moves it left); past sup's wall → sole coverage (800k measured); past lat's ~987k → the same β slides to mem-mode and extends coverage to **~1.5M**.

**Hyperparameters, all four:** β (profile dial) · h (headroom 2–8%, moves every boundary) · N* (knee ≈0.4M tokens) · the per-family affine fits (2 probes each to refit; probe-vs-predict mismatch refits one family — that's the learning loop).

**The one honest gap:** today the dial is a 4-step staircase, not a smooth curve — graded per-layer keep-acts (already designed as D3-graded) would make it genuinely continuous. Everything else is measured crossings, not hand-tuned thresholds.

**1. Yes — and "clean" here has a precise meaning: the configs are *nested*.** Knobs are ordered by their measured price ρ (tok/s gained per GiB spent). Raising β sheds knobs strictly in reverse-price order, one breakpoint at a time — never reshuffles, never oscillates (the order is scale-invariant across seq/model, §2.3). So turning the dial walks you down a monotone staircase where each step has a known price tag:

| β (tok/s per GiB) | config emitted | what's kept in GPU vs offloaded |
|---|---|---|
| < 0.87 | **asym-lat** (staged + ker000 + keep-acts) | everything resident: MLP intermediates, attention inputs, recompute-saves all stay in HBM; routing buffers materialized; weight panels staged in |
| 0.87 – 0.90 | shed keep-acts → **balanced** | intermediates now copy out to CPU after forward, copy back for backward (−~36 GiB @120k×8, +32 s) |
| 0.90 – 9.2 | shed ker000 → ker101 | routing buffers never materialized (−36 GiB, +33 s) |
| > 9.2 | shed staged → **asym-mem** | weights computed straight from CPU, no panel staging (−7 GiB, +67 s) |
| (any β, host-pressured) | + ohbm | checkpoint anchors HBM↔host — separate host-side dial |

The one granularity gap I'll flag again: keep-acts is currently all-or-nothing; the designed per-layer version (keep the *last* k layers' tensors first — provably the right order, since early layers' tensors sit in memory longest) would turn that big step into a smooth ramp. That's the only build needed for a truly continuous dial.

**2. Correct — batch is an output, never an input.** You give (model, seq); the scheduler computes, per family:

```
B* = min( B_knee(s),  B_max(s) )
      B_knee = ceil(N*/s)            smallest batch that saturates the GPU (knee ≈ 0.4M tokens for q3-30b)
      B_max  = largest healthy batch = floor((C_eff − base)/(m·s)), ≤92% HBM
```

Below the knee, batch buys real throughput → the leaner family (asym) wins by fitting more batch — that's the 120k×8 +23%. Above the knee, tok/s is batch-flat (measured b2=b4=b5), so it deliberately picks the *smallest* saturating batch and banks the freed memory — which the β·M term rewards. So the same two lines produce "big batch at short seq, b1 at ultra-long" without anyone choosing a batch by hand.

[2026-07-19T11:27:45.517Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**The knob is β (beta) — a price.** One number, in units of **"tok/s you're willing to give up to keep 1 GiB of GPU memory free."**

What tuning it means, in words:
- **β = 0**: "memory is free, I only care about speed" → the scheduler picks the fastest config that physically fits, even at 98% memory.
- **β = 2** (default-ish): "I'll sacrifice up to 2 tok/s per GiB freed" → still speed-first, but ties break to the leaner config and it won't ride the memory edge.
- **β = 50**: "memory is precious" → it accepts big slowdowns to keep memory low → you get memory mode.

How the decision actually happens — no thresholds are set by hand. Every optimization we have (keep activations on GPU, materialize routing buffers, stage weight panels…) was **measured** to have a price tag ρ = "tok/s it buys per GiB it costs." Examples: staged panels buy ~9.2 per GiB, keep-acts buys ~0.87 per GiB. The rule is one comparison:

> **turn an optimization ON iff its ρ ≥ your β** (i.e., it buys speed at a better rate than the price you set) — and it still fits.

So the "thresholds" you asked about aren't tuned — **they are the measured ρ values of the knobs.** β is the only thing you set, and moving it across a knob's ρ is exactly the moment that knob switches off. Setting β low = latency-focused profile; high = memory-focused; the configs change in a fixed, nested order in between.

====================================================================================================
Reasoned through it — **your critique is correct and it changes the exposed knob, not the math.** Full design written to `agent/handoffs/prompt.md`; `scheduler_v2.md` §9.5 updated to defer to it. The answer:

**The right knob is a memory budget, not a price.** β (tok/s-per-GiB) and a budget M* are mathematical duals — they trace the same frontier — but only one is usable:

| | β (price) | **hbm_budget (GiB or %)** |
|---|---|---|
| user can calibrate it? | no — no real-world referent | yes — it's the nvidia-smi number |
| hardware-portable? | no — range shifts with every GPU/model | yes (as %) |
| verifiable? | no | yes: peak-reserved ≤ budget, check it |

**Final interface — two physical knobs, both optional:**
1. **`hbm_budget`** (default = whole device): the latency↔memory steering wheel. 100% = most-latency-focused the workload allows; 55% = memory-focused. Lowering it sheds optimizations in one fixed, measured order (staged → ker000 → keep-acts) — nested configs, monotone, never oscillates.
2. **`safety`** ∈ {conservative/normal/aggressive} = 8/5/2% edge headroom — the only other genuine user preference the data supports (the measured penalty structure has exactly 3 regimes).

Users never pick modes, batches, or prices — **batch and mode are outputs** (B\* = min(knee, capacity); "latency/memory mode" become labels on the emitted config). β survives only as the baked-in ladder *order*.

**And the key structural insight your question exposed:** for your stated goal — parity at mid seqs, real advantage at ultra-long — **no user knob needs touching at all.** At default budget, the orientation over (model, seq) is the shadow of the fit constraint tightening: short → full latency stack wins (+6–23%), mid → sup fallback emerges (parity by construction), 640k+ → asym parity→win, past the walls → sole coverage, and past asym-lat's own ~990k the ladder sheds itself down to asym-mem, extending coverage to ~1.5M. The budget knob exists for when memory has *external* value (co-tenant, serving job, margin) — which is the only situation where a latency↔memory preference is even meaningful.

[2026-07-19T11:41:03.013Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**The formulation that survives review** (recorded as v2 in `agent/handoffs/prompt.md`):

**Drop the preference knob entirely. The scheduler is an *allocator*, not a dial.** HBM is a fixed endowment that is always fully spent — the only real question is *what to spend it on*, and there are exactly two productive assets, with measured returns:

| asset | cost | return |
|---|---|---|
| **batch units** (+1 sample) | m·s GiB each | big below the knee (~0.4M tokens), **≈0 above** (measured b2=b4=b5) |
| **residency knobs** (staged panels, route buffers, keep-acts) | ∝ tokens | per-token time saved (measured ρ ladder) |

**The whole scheduler = one greedy water-fill:** repeatedly buy the single next unit — one more sample *or* one more knob — with the highest marginal Δtok/s per GiB, until the device is full or returns hit zero; argmax across families (sup fallback included). One ranking, zero preference parameters. This also *unifies* what were two separate rules: B\*=min(knee, capacity) stops being a rule and becomes a theorem (batch prices itself out of the ranking at the knee), and "larger batch instead of thrashing" is literally the allocator outbidding residency with batch at short seq while refusing >98% rows that lose tok/s.

**"Latency-focused vs memory-focused" becomes the *output*, steered by (model, seq) exactly as you asked:** short seq → the portfolio comes out batch+residency-rich (reads as latency mode, +6–23% vs baselines); mid → residency-only at knee-batch, sup wins argmax → parity; ultra-long → the allocator can't afford residency and sheds it in ladder order → memory mode emerges, sole coverage to ~1.5M. Nobody sets an orientation; the workload does.

**What's left user-facing:** nothing preferential — just `safety` (2/5/8% headroom = risk, not preference) and an optional `reserved_hbm` (default 0, the multi-tenant carve-out — the *only* legitimate remnant of the budget idea). Rejected alternatives are ledgered with reasons: β-price (uncalibratable), budget-as-primary (nobody limits HBM — your point), Pareto-menu (pushes the decision back to the user; kept as a report), SLO-inverse (serving, not training).

This is, I'd argue, the defensible novelty for a systems write-up: *batch and kernel/residency choices competing in a single measured marginal-return ranking, with training "modes" as emergent portfolios* — every constant in it fitted from probes, every regime boundary it predicts independently confirmed by the c14 campaign.

[2026-07-19T21:19:14.534Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**The scheduler in one idea:** GPU memory is a fixed budget that's always fully spent — the only question is *what to spend it on*. There are exactly two things worth buying, each with a measured return:

1. **Batch** (+1 sample costs m·s GiB) — big throughput return below the saturation knee (~0.4M tokens/step), ~zero above it (measured: tok/s batch-flat).
2. **Residency optimizations** (staged weight panels, ker000 route buffers, keep-activations-in-HBM) — each saves a measured number of us/token and costs GiB proportional to tokens.

**The algorithm:** start bare (b1, nothing on) and greedily buy whichever single unit — one more sample or the next optimization — gives the most tok/s per GiB, until memory is full or returns hit zero. Do this per backend family (asym, sup-unsloth, sup-recomp) and emit the fastest. All constants come from fitted probe data; when a run disagrees with prediction, refit that family (self-calibrating — the 900k run just did this).

**Consequences, all emergent (no if-else, no user knob):**
- Short seq → buys lots of batch + all optimizations = "latency mode", beats baselines +6–23%
- Mid seq → superoffload wins argmax = **fallback**, baseline preserved exactly
- Long seq → asym latency mode, parity→sole coverage (640k–880k)
- Ultra-long → can't afford keep-acts → sheds optimizations in fixed reverse-value order = "balanced"→"memory mode", coverage to ~1.5M

**User inputs:** model + seq. Batch, mode, config = outputs. Only knobs: `safety` (2/5/8% headroom, risk not preference) and optional `reserved_hbm` (multi-tenant carve-out). "Latency/memory mode" are labels the system prints, never things you set. Verified: 5/5 cleanness properties (nested, monotone, fixed shed order) + the 900k GPU run within 3% of prediction.

Yes, exactly right — the *configs* are discrete. There are only 4 flag-rungs (staged → ker000 → keep-acts → panel-cache), so per family you get ~5 distinct configs, from all-off (= memory mode) to all-on (= latency mode). Flipping them on = more latency-focused, off = more memory-focused.

What the scheduler adds is just the *decision rule* for which discrete point to pick: the flags have a fixed value-order (measured tok/s-per-GiB), so it flips them on greedily in that order — batch competes for the same memory — until the budget's spent. That's why the output walks down discrete steps as seq grows (all 4 on → drop panel-cache → drop keep-acts → …), never some in-between blend.

So: **discrete menu, continuous selector.** The only thing that would make the dial itself continuous is the designed-but-unbuilt per-layer keep-acts (keep last k layers instead of all-or-nothing); until then it's a staircase with ~5 steps, and that's what the 5/5 selftest properties certify — the steps always come in the same nested order, no weird mixes.

[2026-07-19T21:45:33.415Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**1. How the flags flip (the mechanism):** each flag buys speed but costs memory that **grows with sequence length** (its tensors scale with tokens). The scheduler turns flags on in fixed value-order (staged → ker000 → keep-acts → panel-cache) *as long as they still fit*. As seq grows, the expensive flags stop fitting and drop off **in reverse order** — that drop-off IS the latency→memory transition. Nobody flips anything; the fit test does.

**2. The consequences, with real numbers** (asym, b1, from the calibrated model — the table above):

| seq | flags that fit | tok/s (bare → best-fitting) | what you lose vs full stack |
|---|---|---|---|
| 480k | **all 4** (103 GiB) | 836 → **947** | nothing — full latency mode, +13% over bare |
| 900k | keep-acts no longer fits (would be ~177–183 GiB) → staged+ker000 | 498 → **525** | ~2% (534 unreachable) |
| 1000k | same, balanced | 454 → **476** | ~2% |
| 1300k | ker000 drops too → staged only | 359 → **368** | ~3% |

Two takeaways: the flags are worth **+6–13% tok/s** when affordable (staged is the big one, +50 tok/s-class; the rest are smaller), and the *cost of shedding them is mild* (~2–3%) — the real story at ultra-long is that shedding is what lets asym **run at all** (superoffload is OOM-dead past 660k regardless of flags). Note 900k is the boundary case: normal safety sheds keep-acts, but our actual GPU run kept it at aggressive-edge (98.9%, 519 tok/s measured) — both choices are within ~3% of each other, which is why the boundary position is low-stakes.

[2026-07-19T21:47:17.484Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Sorry — plain words:

**1.** In that table, each row of "flags that fit" compared two configs:
- "bare" = **all 4 optimization flags OFF** (the slowest, least-memory config)
- "best-fitting" = **as many flags ON as memory allows at that sequence length** (the fastest config that doesn't run out of GPU memory)

So "836 → 947 @480k" meant: flags all off = 836 tok/s; the best config that fits (all 4 on) = 947 tok/s.

**2.** "Shed" = **turn a flag off**. Nothing more. The sentence "keep-acts is shed at 900k" just means: at 900k sequence length, the keep-activations-on-GPU flag would need more memory than the GPU has, so the scheduler turns that flag off and runs without it.

The whole system restated without any invented words: there are 4 optimization flags, each makes training faster but uses more GPU memory, and their memory use grows with sequence length. For a given model + sequence length, the scheduler turns on every flag that still fits in memory (in a fixed priority order), picks the batch size the same way, compares the result against the plain superoffload baselines, and runs whichever is fastest. Short sequences → all flags on (fastest configuration). Very long sequences → flags get turned off one by one because they no longer fit — the price is small (~2–3% each) and it's what lets training keep working at lengths where the baselines crash.

The 4 flags, concretely (all in the asym backend; each = faster but more GPU memory):

**1. `ASYM_GEMM_DISPATCH=staged`** — *where matrix multiplies read weights from.*
The base model's weights live in CPU RAM (that's the backend's whole premise). OFF: a custom kernel computes directly against CPU-resident weights over the interconnect — no GPU copy, but ~3× slower than a normal matmul. ON: each weight matrix is first copied CPU→GPU (~0.4–2 GiB at a time), then multiplied with the normal fast cuBLAS kernel. Cost: ~2 GiB. Gain: the biggest of all — ~70 us per token.

**2. `ker000` (vs `ker101`)** — *how tokens get routed to MoE experts.*
A MoE layer must group each token with its chosen experts. `ker101` (OFF-state): fused custom kernels do the routing math inside the matmul without ever building the big intermediate tensor. `ker000` (ON-state): explicitly materializes the routed copy of activations — one row per (token × expert) — in GPU memory, then uses plain fast kernels on it. Cost: ~0.04 GiB per 1k tokens (~36 GiB at 120k×8). Gain: ~34 us/token.

**3. keep-acts = `ASYMM_QWEN3_MOE_FG_KEEP_ACTS_HBM=1` + `ASYMM_ATTN_ACT_KEEP_ACTS_HBM=1` + `ASYM_GC_SAVE_ON_CPU_OVERRIDE=false`** — *where saved activations wait between forward and backward.*
Backward needs forward's intermediate results (MLP gate/up outputs, attention projection inputs, checkpoint tensors). OFF: right after forward, copy them GPU→CPU to free memory, copy back at backward — two big transfers per layer, GPU often waiting. ON: they just stay in GPU memory. Cost: ~0.05 GiB per 1k tokens (the biggest memory eater; ~52 GiB at 1M tokens). Gain: ~33 us/token.

**4. `ASYM_W_PANEL_CACHE_GB=6`** — *don't re-upload identical weights.*
With staged dispatch, the same frozen weight block gets copied CPU→GPU up to 12× per layer per step (forward, recompute, backward passes). ON: a 6-GiB cache on GPU remembers recently uploaded blocks and skips repeat copies. Cost: exactly 6 GiB. Gain: small, ~3 us/token.

**Latency↔memory tuning = how many of these are on**, always in this order (best value first: 1→2→3→4 on the way to latency; 4→3→2→1 off on the way to memory). All 4 on = "latency mode" (fastest, most memory). All off = "memory mode": every multiply streams from CPU, routing never materializes, activations round-trip to CPU — slowest (~10–13% slower total) but the leanest per-token memory, which is what reaches ~1.5M-token sequences.

All four questions, concisely:

**1. Correct — 1 and 2 are not independent.** The `ker101` fused-routing kernels only exist in the custom (asym) engine; under `staged` dispatch everything runs through standard torch kernels, so routing must be materialized (`ker000`). Legal combos are effectively 3, not 4: asym-engine+ker101 (leanest) → staged+ker101-style-lean is *not* available → staged+ker000 → +keep-acts. The ladder respects that: ker000 only turns on together-with-or-after staged, and on the way down, dropping staged forces ker101 back. So it's a nested chain, not a free 2×2 grid. (In the scheduler's constants ker000's cost/gain is measured *conditional on staged already being on* — exactly because of this coupling.)

**2. Good instinct, but "fused is faster" assumes equal engines — here fusion is tied to the slow engine.** ker101's fusion does save memory *and* avoids the routing kernels' time, but it runs inside the custom streamed-GEMM engine whose matmuls are ~3× slower than cuBLAS. Measured net (@120k×8): staged+ker000 beats asym+ker101 by ~32 s/step despite materializing +36 GiB. Fusion wins *within* an engine; it loses when it costs you the fast engine. (A fused route on top of cuBLAS would be the best of both — that kernel doesn't exist today; it's the C1b-class future work.)

**3. Mostly yes.** This config runs full gradient-checkpointing, so each layer's "forward" executes twice — once in the real forward (activations discarded), once as recompute inside backward. Flags 1/2/4 apply to *both* executions (they're about every matmul/routing call). Flag 3 (keep-acts) applies specifically to the recompute pass — the tensors saved between a layer's recompute and its backward — plus the attention projection inputs and checkpoint boundary tensors. Peak memory is set inside the backward window, which is why keep-acts' cost lands there.

**4. Yes — flag 4 is just a bounded reuse buffer**: a 6-GiB LRU keyed by weight pointer; hit = skip the CPU→GPU copy, miss = copy and insert, evict oldest when full. Frozen weights never change, so there's no coherence problem. Nothing subtle beyond that.

| set | what it is | speed price when OFF | memory saved when OFF |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Set C — weight-reupload cache** (`ASYM_W_PANEL_CACHE_GB`) | skip repeat CPU→GPU weight copies | ~3 us/tok | 6 GiB flat |
| **Set B — keep-acts** (the 3 activation-residency flags) | saved activations stay on GPU vs round-trip to CPU | ~33 us/tok | ~0.05 GiB per 1k tokens (the big one at long seq) |
| **Set A — engine bundle** (`staged`+`ker000` vs `asym`+`ker101`) | fast cuBLAS on staged weights + materialized routing vs slow streamed kernels + fused routing | ~104 us/tok | ~2 GiB + 0.04 GiB per 1k tokens |

Latency mode = A+B+C all on. Turn off C → B → A in that order: each step is strictly slower and strictly leaner. That's the entire dial — 4 positions.

That's why A is one set, not two.

[2026-07-19T22:17:10.339Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**1. Why turn off in the order C → B → A?** One principle: **speed-value per GiB of memory** — when memory gets tight, drop the flag that buys the least speed per GiB it occupies, keep the best deal until last. With the measured prices (at ~900k, b1):

| set | speed it buys | memory it costs | value density |
|---|---|---|---|
| C cache | 3 us/tok | 6 GiB | **0.5** us/tok per GiB → drop 1st |
| B keep-acts | 33 us/tok | ~47 GiB | **0.7** → drop 2nd |
| A engine | 104 us/tok | ~36 GiB | **2.9** → keep to the end |

Drop order = ascending value density. It's not hand-chosen — it's computed from the measured prices, and it happens to stay the same order across all seq lengths (A's density dominates everywhere because its speed gain is huge relative to its memory). If a future kernel changed the prices, the order would recompute. That's the entire justification: it's a knapsack — evict the worst deal first.

**4. Correct.** C1b has nothing "asym" left in it — weights would already be staged to GPU. It's just a **standard fused MoE routing kernel over normal GEMMs** (the same idea vLLM/Megatron-style fused dispatch kernels use): do the token→expert gather/scatter inside the kernel instead of materializing the routed tensor. Building it would give Set A's speed *and* ker101's memory simultaneously — Set A's tradeoff would disappear.

**5. Remaining future work, each self-contained:**

1. **C1b fused routing on the fast path** — as above; kills the +36 GiB routing-buffer cost while keeping cuBLAS speed.
2. **Per-layer keep-acts** — today Set B keeps *all 64 layers'* saved activations on GPU or none. Instead keep only the last k layers (backward needs those first; the earliest layers wait longest and are the cheapest to offload). Sliding k from 64→0 turns the one big memory step into a smooth dial.
3. **GPU buffer pool** — torch's allocator fragments with many large, varied allocations: we measured 62 GiB *reserved but unusable* at 208k b5. Pre-allocating fixed, recycled buffers (Megatron-style) reclaims that → 2–3 more samples of batch at the same seq.
4. **Copy prefetch/overlap** — when backward needs a CPU-offloaded tensor, today the copy starts on demand and the GPU partially waits. Prefetch = start the copy one layer ahead on a separate channel so data is already there; same for outbound copies. Worth ~5–8 us/tok of the remaining gap.
5. **Re-profile memory mode** — all asym-mem numbers (including the ~1.5M ceiling claim) predate the 5 fixes; re-measure speed/capacity on current source so the scheduler's leanest rung uses honest constants.
6. **Finish the 1.1M validation run** — the interrupted balanced-mode run: staged+ker000 only, expect ~436 tok/s and ~158–175 GiB; confirms the scheduler's first shed decision on real hardware.

**1a.** Yes — Set A ON = copy the weight block to GPU and use normal cuBLAS; OFF = the project's custom asym kernel computing directly against CPU-resident weights. That engine choice is the project's core primitive.

**1b.** Yes — keep-acts is essentially **adopting unsloth's residency policy** inside asym's own machinery. In this codebase "unsloth" mode literally means recompute-saved activations stay in GPU memory; our flag makes asym's recompute wrapper do the same (and one of its three sub-flags is even just "use unsloth's save-on-CPU=false setting"). The difference is only *whose* wrapper the policy is applied to.

**1c.** Yes — a plain LRU dict keyed by weight pointer, capped in GiB. Nothing more.

**4.** After C1b the matchup is fused-MoE-on-normal-GEMM (staged weights) vs fused-asym-MoE (CPU weights) — and the point is that **today's 36 GiB memory difference is NOT from weight staging; it's from routing materialization**, which C1b eliminates. Weight staging itself only costs ~0.4–2 GiB transient (one panel at a time) + optional cache. So yes: post-C1b the memory gap between the two engines shrinks to a couple of GiB, and the remaining tradeoff (fast-GPU-multiply vs zero-staging-traffic) is nearly free to pick.

**5. Honest split — most mechanisms are engineering; three things are defensible as research:**

| item | status |
|---|---|
| activation offload to CPU + side-stream prefetch | **engineering** — DeepSpeed ZeRO-Offload/Infinity, Megatron `fine_grained_activation_offload` do this |
| weight streaming/staging from CPU, LRU weight cache | **engineering** — ZeRO-Infinity, FlexGen lineage |
| fused MoE routing kernels (C1b) | **engineering** — vLLM/SGLang/Megatron grouped-GEMM dispatch kernels |
| GPU buffer pool | **engineering** — Megatron's `GPUTensorPool` verbatim |
| per-layer graded keep-acts | mostly engineering — selective/partial checkpointing exists |
| **the asym GEMM primitive** (dense compute *directly* against CPU-resident weights over the C2C link, no staging) | **research** — the project's novel kernel; nobody's frameworks do the multiply in-place from host memory as a first-class training path |
| **the scheduler as formulated** (measured affine cost model + one knapsack over batch+residency assets + emergent modes + baseline fallback + predict-probe-refit loop) | **research-able** — existing autotuners (DeepSpeed autotune, Alpa/FlexFlow for parallelism) are search-based or target different decision spaces; a closed-form, measurement-calibrated allocator with provable nested/monotone behavior is a legitimate systems contribution |
| **the empirical frontier map** (walls per config, batch-flat knee law, edge-penalty regimes, the parity crossover + sole-coverage window) | **research** as measurement/characterization — it's the evidence that makes the scheduler's claims falsifiable |

So the paper story isn't any single flag — it's: novel kernel primitive at the bottom, principled measured allocator on top, and the measured frontier proving the system extends trainable sequence length ~2.3× past the strongest baseline at ≤3% cost where the baseline exists at all.

Doc written. Now the two answers, concisely:

**1b — not literally the same.** "Unsloth with asym" as a config isn't the shipped path: asym's recompute *must* run through its own fine-grained wrapper (that wrapper IS the machinery that makes LoRA-on-CPU-weights work — keep-acts is implemented inside it). Keep-acts copies **unsloth's residency *policy*** ("recompute-saves stay on GPU") into that wrapper — same idea, different machinery. So: same policy, not the same code path, and plain `asym|unsloth` without the wrapper would lose the CPU-weight plumbing.

**4 — your confusion is justified; two completely separate systems were being mixed:**
- Everything I said about staged/ker000/ker101/grouped-mm is **inside the asym backend only** — it's about *our* expert GEMMs when base weights live in CPU RAM. (And yes, our staged path *does* use `torch grouped_mm`; superoffload doesn't need any of this — it runs the stock HF expert path at full GPU speed on weights its own DeepSpeed machinery manages.)
- **superoffload|unsloth-off's memory saving has nothing to do with asym kernels.** It's pure activation offload *within the baseline*: `unsloth-off` = save recompute activations to CPU instead of GPU. That's their lever.
- **Asym's memory advantage** comes from its own two things: base weights never resident on GPU (the asym kernel / transient staged panels), and its fine-grained activation machinery. So: baselines save memory with *their* offload; we save more with *ours*; the flag discussion was only ever about tuning ours.

**5 — recorded.** `agent/impls/remaining_optimizations.md` now holds the summary table up top (8 items: what each buys, engineering-vs-research class, effort, blockers) with self-contained detail sections below, including the honest research/engineering split (asym GEMM primitive + scheduler formulation + frontier map = research; the rest = adoption of DeepSpeed/Megatron/vLLM-class techniques).

how do i interpere the 3 mus/tok what doe that mean?

====================================================================================================
[2026-07-19T22:54:05.234Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**us/tok = microseconds of step time per token processed** — the per-token cost of a training step. It's just: step time ÷ tokens in the step. Example: 900k tokens at 1733 s/step → 1733s/900k ≈ 1926 us/tok.

It's the right unit here because at long sequences throughput is per-token-limited, so costs *add linearly* in this unit and convert directly:

- "the panel cache saves 3 us/tok" → at 480k tokens/step, saves 3 × 480k = 1.44 s per step
- tok/s = 1,000,000 ÷ (us/tok) → shaving 33 us/tok (keep-acts) off ~1030 us/tok at 480k is what took 948 → ~975 tok/s

So when you see "flag X buys 33 us/tok, flag Y buys 3": every token gets cheaper by that many microseconds, multiply by tokens-per-step for seconds saved, and smaller us/tok = faster. It also makes comparisons seq-independent — sup vs asym at "+143 us/tok backward tax" means the same thing at any sequence length, whereas "+55 s/step" only means something at one specific seq.

[2026-07-19T23:33:10.291Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Not a fallback relationship — they're **two independent backends**, and the scheduler picks whichever wins at the given seq:

**What's actually different (one thing, fundamentally):** where the frozen base weights live and who manages movement.
- **so-unsloth** = DeepSpeed superoffload: weights paged/streamed by ZeRO-style machinery, expert compute via the stock HF path, unsloth checkpointing (saves stay on GPU).
- **asym T1** = our backend: weights *permanently* in CPU RAM, staged panel-by-panel per use (or computed straight from CPU in lower tiers), our own fine-grained LoRA wrapper + CPU AdamW, same keep-saves-on-GPU policy, grouped-mm experts.

**Consequence:** asym carries ~4 GiB base vs sup's ~20, and ~0.18 vs 0.25 GiB per 1k tokens — that's why asym holds bigger batches at equal seq, survives to ~990k vs sup's 660k, and why its walls are deeper. Price: a small per-token tax (−1.5% @480k post-fixes, parity by 640k).

**On "fallback":** it's the reverse of what you said — **asym is the primary system; sup-unsloth is the fallback**, emitted only in the 160–600k window where its tax-free path is still marginally faster. Short seqs (asym wins on batch) and long seqs (asym wins on capacity) are asym's outright.
