====================================================================================================
Yes — you've got it right, and I should say it plainly: **mechanistically T1 and so-unsloth are the same design point.** Host-resident frozen weights, staged to GPU on demand, fast native GEMMs, recompute-saves kept on GPU, optimizer on CPU. Our whole fix campaign was literally *removing* asym's accidental differences (extra CPU round-trips) — converging it onto that shared mechanism. The distinctive asym primitive (computing *directly* from CPU weights, no staging) only lives in T3/memory mode.

The differences that remain in T1 are implementation-level, not mechanism-level — but they're measurable and they're the point:
- **leaner residency**: ~4 GiB base vs ~20, 0.179 vs 0.253 GiB per 1k tokens (DeepSpeed keeps bigger resident working sets/prefetch buffers) → wall at ~990k vs 660k, more batch at equal seq
- **~1.5–4% speed tax** the other way (their path is still a hair faster mid-window)

So the honest framing: **T1 = our implementation of the superoffload-class mechanism, leaner but marginally slower; the "fallback" between them is choosing between two implementations of the same idea, worth a few % either way.** The *system's* real novelty is the ends of the dial — T3's stage-free kernel (capacity) and the scheduler that walks T1→T2→T3 as seq grows — not T1 vs sup, which is, as you say, essentially the same behavior.

| tier | your reading | precise version |
|---|---|---|
| **T1 LATENCY** | "get on par with recomp/unsloth" | Slightly better: **parity is the floor, not the goal**. Mid-band (160–600k) it's parity (−1.5…−4%, fallback covers it). But short (<130k) T1 *beats* the baselines outright (+6–23%), and 600–660k it matches them while they ride their 98% edge. And T1's band already extends *past* their capacity (660k→900k = sole coverage) — so T1 isn't only "match them where they exist." |
| **T2 BALANCED** | "beyond capacity but still be fast" | ✅ Exactly. All of T2's range (900k–1.25M) is past every baseline's wall; the only competition is our own T3, and T2 keeps the fast GEMMs (+ ~7–8% over what T3 would give there) at moderate memory. |
| **T3 MEMORY** | "aim only capacity" | ✅ Yes. Nothing else reaches 1.25M+, and its stage-free kernel + fused routing is the leanest per token — pure max-sequence (and max-batch-per-GiB) play. Speed is whatever it is (~20–25% below T2's rate). |

So the one-line summary: T1 = win-or-match wherever baselines exist and stretch 240k past them; T2 = keep speed in no-baseline territory; T3 = pure capacity frontier.

====================================================================================================
Your instinct is right, and it's worth being precise about *where* the +240k comes from — the two measured components have different defensibility:

1. **Fixed overhead (~15 GiB): pure implementation disparity.** DeepSpeed's machinery keeps a bigger resident working set (partitions, prefetch buffers). A DeepSpeed patch could claw much of this back. **Not defensible as a contribution — downplay.**
2. **Per-token slope (0.179 vs 0.253 GiB/1k, ~30% leaner): partly a real design choice.** Both keep recompute-saves on GPU, but *what* they save differs: our `recomp-off-full-fg` does **finer-grained recomputation** — saves a smaller per-layer set (compact/low-rank intermediates, bounded chunks) and re-derives more during backward — while unsloth's stock path checkpoints a heavier per-layer set. "Finer recompute granularity + selective residency → 30% leaner at equal speed" is a legitimate design claim — but it's an optimization *within* the same mechanism class, and a motivated baseline team could adopt it too.

**So for the paper: yes, downplay the T1-vs-sup wall.** Frame it as "even our staged tier, being a leaner implementation of the same mechanism, incidentally extends coverage ~36%" — one sentence, honest about impl-dependence. The **defensible capacity story stays where the mechanism actually differs**: T3's stage-free kernel (+118% at b8, ceilings no staged system can reach), the scheduler that gets you there automatically, and the measured frontier map. T1's job in the narrative is speed (win short, parity mid), not capacity.

All three asym tiers share the same `recomp-off-full-fg` recompute *structure*; the tiers only differ in engine (staged/asym), routing (ker000/ker101), and **where** the saved set lives (keep-acts = HBM vs CPU).

The key distinction: keep-acts changes *where* the saved tensors sit, not *what* gets saved. The fine-grained design — save a small set (compact X, low-rank S, chunk-bounded transients), re-derive the rest during backward — is active in T1 too. That's exactly why T1's measured per-token slope (0.179 GiB/1k) is ~30% leaner than unsloth's (0.253) *even though both keep their saves in GPU memory*: we're keeping a smaller set.

So the earlier point stands as stated: T1's capacity edge = ~15 GiB impl overhead (not defensible) + the leaner-saved-set design (semi-defensible, same mechanism class) — and both are present in latency mode.

Yes — correct, and the measured copies prove it. Even in T1 with keep-acts on, asym still moves **more bytes** than sup: weight panels are re-staged per pass (~560 GB/step at 208k vs sup's leaner prefetched streaming), and a residual saved-tensor round-trip (~400 GB/step class) survives — total memcpy ~15–18 us/tok vs sup's ~4.5 in the twin trace.

So the sharp statement: **same mechanism *class* (host-resident weights + streaming + fast GPU compute + saves-mostly-on-GPU), but not the same point in it.** The two implementations sit at different residency-vs-traffic balances:

- **sup-unsloth:** holds more resident (bigger working set, heavier saved set) → moves less → a hair faster
- **asym T1:** holds less resident (leaner saved set, transient panels) → moves more → −1.5–4% slower, but ~30% leaner per token

And note these are *the same coin*: the capacity edge and the speed tax both come from holding less and moving more. That's why the honest paper framing is: T1 = a different operating point on the same residency↔traffic spectrum (leaner, marginally slower), the scheduler picks per workload — and the *mechanistic* novelty claims stay with T3's stage-free kernel and the scheduler itself.

[2026-07-20T00:41:02.313Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**1. No, the build won't affect run latency** — verified empirically, not just assumed: we ran builds alongside GPU runs before (the 480k/600k builds during the recomp 320k run) and specifically checked — step times/MFU stayed on trend. Reasons: builds run at `nice -19` (lowest CPU priority), use 1–2 of the 144 cores, and the training step at these seqs is GPU/transfer-bound, not CPU-starved.

**Why 50 min and not a few minutes — because the builder is naive, not because the work is big:** it assembles each sample by concatenating text and *re-tokenizing to count tokens* until it hits the length target, single-threaded, then writes ~3 GB of JSONL to the ~99%-full NFS. That's ~250k tokens/s effective. The tokenization itself (0.7B tokens for 512×1.4M) would be ~5–10 min with batched/parallel tokenization to local disk — so yes, a ~5–10× speedup is easy engineering. I haven't done it because the build sits entirely off the critical path (it hides inside R1's window), so it would buy zero wall-clock for this campaign.

**2. No caching action needed from you:**
- **Tokenizer + model weights**: already cached node-local (`HF_HOME=/scratch_local/.../huggingface`) — no re-downloads.
- **Built datasets**: the JSONL files *are* the cache — content-deterministic, reused forever via `DATASET_OVERWRITE=false` (all seqs through 1.1M already exist; only s1400000 is new).
- The one small residual: LlamaFactory re-tokenizes the dataset at each run start (part of the ~10–15 min load phase you see before step 0). That could also be cached, but it's the same cost for every backend equally, so it doesn't touch any comparison.

Queue unchanged and ready: R1 → R2 → R3 → R4, ~11.6 h total. Fire?

[2026-07-20T01:10:25.263Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Almost — it's the reverse ratio: **1 warmup + N measured** (warmup first, then measured), never 4 warmups.

- Earlier campaign runs: `WARMUP_STEPS=1 MAX_STEPS=4` → **5 total steps** = 1 warmup + 4 measured.
- The current ultra-long queue (R1–R4): `WARMUP_STEPS=1 MAX_STEPS=3` → **4 total steps** = 1 warmup + 3 measured (trimmed because steps cost ~20–40+ min each at these seqs; 3 measured still gives a stable middle).

The reported s/it always **excludes the warmup** (protocol: steady = the measured steps' middle — first step pays one-time init like allocator warmup, cache fills, so it's dropped). Memory peaks are taken across the whole run, so nothing is lost there.

[2026-07-20T20:01:15.649Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Yes — we have exactly that, and it's paper-ready. The formal system (in `scheduler_v2.md` §9 + `agent/handoffs/prompt.md` v2, validated in code): given model M and sequence s, with **two fitted affine cost models per config family** x:

```
τ_x(s)  = a_x + b·s                 (per-token step time, us/tok; b = shared attention slope)
M_x(s,B) = base_x + B·m_x·s          (peak HBM, GiB; analogous D_x for host RAM)
```

**the scheduler is one argmax:**

```
x*(M, s) = argmax_x  TP(x) = 10⁶/τ_x(s) · pen(u)     s.t.  M_x ≤ (1−h)·C,  D_x ≤ D_wall
B* = min( ⌈N*/s⌉ , B_max(s) )        (knee law: tok/s is batch-flat above N* ≈ 0.4M tokens — measured)
```

where x ranges over {superoffload, asym} × the **nested knob ladder** (staged → ker000 → keep-acts, admitted in fixed measured value-per-GiB order ρ = 2.9 / 0.9 / 0.7), pen(u) is the measured edge-penalty step function (0 below 92% utilization, ~4% to 98%, ∞ above), and h is the only tunable (headroom 2–8%).

**The "modes" are then theorems, not settings** — each boundary is a closed-form budget crossing, e.g. the T1→T2 boundary is just `s* = (C(1−h) − base − Σdm_fixed)/(m + Σdm_tok)`. For q3-30b that yields T1 < ~900k < T2 < ~1.25M < T3 — and the *fallback to superoffload is also emergent* (sup wins the argmax at 160–600k because a_sup < a_asym there; every asym per-token fix moves that window automatically).

**Its paper-grade credentials:** all constants fitted from 2 probes/family; predictions validated blind (walls predicted 638k/391k vs measured (640k,660k]/(392k,400k]; the 900k emission fit at −3% tok/s error); the formulation has machine-checked structural properties (nested/monotone config shedding — `asym_scheduler.py --selftest`, 5/5); and a predict→probe→refit loop as the honest calibration story. Batch can indeed stay manual if you prefer — B* is a one-line heuristic on top, severable from the mode selection.

[2026-07-20T21:50:48.234Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**The concise answer:**

1. **Mode/tier decisions never touch us/tok.** T1→T2→T3 boundaries are pure byte thresholds — `s* = (available HBM − fixed costs)/(bytes-per-token slope)` — where capacity is a device *spec* and the slopes are derivable from the *model architecture* (h, L, experts, attention type). Bytes are machine-independent: our c12-vs-c14 confirms showed peak-reserved memory **bit-identical** across machines. So the core heuristic is exactly the thresholding form you're describing, and fully hardware-agnostic.

2. **Batch** = same byte arithmetic + one model constant (the knee, a property of the model's compute intensity, not the host).

3. **The only timing-dependent decision is the sup-fallback window** — and it depends only on the *sign/ordering* of the per-token intercepts (which config is faster), not their absolute values; orderings are stable within a hardware class. It's also worth just ±2–4% post-fixes — the degenerate policy "skip timing, always emit asym" loses at most that, while every capacity/mode decision stays exact.

4. **us/tok's real role is an optional 2-probe calibration** that sharpens the fallback boundary and gives the predicted-tok/s contract on a given machine — and for portability it should be expressed as dimensionless ratios vs the sup baseline, not microseconds.

Recorded as v3 in `agent/handoffs/prompt.md` with the paper framing: *"mode selection is closed-form byte thresholding from model architecture + device capacity; a 2-probe timing calibration optionally refines the baseline-fallback boundary."* (Meanwhile 122B cluster B is still running on GPU — uns wall pair first.)

[2026-07-20T22:10:58.296Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Yes — that's essentially the whole scheduler. Precisely:

**Per (model, config) you fit two straight lines from past runs** (2+ runs each):

1. **Memory line** (GiB): `M = base + m · (B·s)` — linear in *tokens in flight*. (Measured to be near-exact: predictions hit within 0.5 GiB, and it's machine-independent — bytes are bytes.)
2. **Time line** (us per token): `τ = a + b·s` — intercept `a` = the config's fixed per-token tax, slope `b` = attention growth.

**Batch is NOT an input — it's derived from line 1:**
```
B* = min(  ⌈N*/s⌉ ,           ← smallest batch that saturates the GPU (knee ≈ 0.4M tokens; more adds nothing — measured)
           ⌊(C·(1−h) − base)/(m·s)⌋ )   ← largest batch that fits
```
(You *may* override it manually; the formula is just this one line.)

**The decision is then:** for every candidate config (sup baselines + the asym tiers, one line-pair each), keep those whose memory line fits under capacity, predict tok/s = 10⁶/τ(s) for each, **pick the max**. Mode boundaries fall out as line crossings — e.g. "T1 ends where T1's memory line hits capacity" gives s* = (C(1−h) − base)/(m + keep-acts slope) ≈ 900k for q3-30b — no thresholds hand-set.

**Caveats, honestly:** (i) it's piecewise — the big-batch regime (below the knee) and the b1 deep-end have different effective τ intercepts, so we anchor short-seq points separately rather than trust one line everywhere; (ii) the time line is per-hardware-class (calibrate with 2 probes; memory line transfers as-is); (iii) each prediction is checked against the actual run and the line refit if off by >tolerance — that's the entire maintenance loop. So: two line-fits per config, batch derived, argmax over lines — that *is* the scheduler.

Two fitted lines per (model, config):
1. **Memory:** `M = base + m·(B·s)` GiB
2. **Speed:** `τ = a + b·s` us/token

**Batch = derived, not entered:** `B* = min(⌈knee/s⌉, largest B that fits line 1)`.

**Decision = argmax:** keep configs whose memory line fits, predict tok/s = 10⁶/τ, pick the fastest. Mode boundaries = where each tier's memory line crosses capacity.

That's the whole scheduler. Fine print: short-seq vs deep-end use separate anchors (piecewise), memory line transfers across machines, speed line needs 2 calibration probes, mispredictions trigger a refit.

| seq | so-recomp | so-unsloth | so-unsloth-OFF | asym T1 | asym T2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **32k b8** | **GPU-OOM** (~181 GiB needed) | 281.8 · **909** · 154.0 (83%) · 659 | **HOST-OOM** (watchdog) | 304.4 · 841 · 113.7 (61%) · 903 | — |
| **320k b1** | OOM* | 499.9 · **640** · 181.3 (98% edge) · 659 — **last fit** | OOM* | ~860 est | — |
| **352k b1** | OOM* | **GPU-OOM → wall (320k, 352k]** | OOM* | — | — |

| **480k b1** | OOM* | OOM | OOM* | GPU-OOM (pred ~193 GiB) | **HOST-OOM** (watchdog 47<50) |

**The story in four lines:**
1. **Crossovers arrive ~10× earlier than q3-30b** — at just 32k×b8, recomp is GPU-dead and unsloth-OFF is host-dead (its streamed 234 GB weights + full act-offload blow the 957 GB node); only plain unsloth survives, with asym at −7.5% and −40 GiB HBM.
2. **so-unsloth's wall = (320k, 352k]**, and it's edge-locked (97–98% HBM) from 288k onward.
3. **asym T1 owns everything beyond**: 874 tok/s @384k and **897 @448k** — *faster at sequences unsloth can't reach at all* (+37–40% over its best-alive 640), because the hybrid linear attention makes asym's per-token cost essentially flat in seq. Max-seq = **448k ≈ 1.36× the unsloth wall**.
4. **asym's own wall @480k is tier-inverted**: T1 runs out of HBM, and T2 (which would normally go deeper) HOST-OOMs instead — on host-bound models keep-acts-OFF *adds* host load, so T1 is the deepest tier. The known lever to push past this: the linear-attention keep-acts port (item 7b), which cuts both the host pools and the 32k gap.

Plot: `figures/out/tp_vs_seq_q3_5-122b-a10b.png`; full log in `test_throughpout_v2.md`.

[2026-07-21T20:17:21.812Z] CLAUDE:

Yes — exactly right, and that's the correction to my worst-case: **sDP (shared-weight data parallel) and sEP (shared/partitioned expert parallel) are the intended asym multi-rank models**, and they exist precisely because asym's host weights are frozen/read-only:

- **sDP**: both ranks stream/stage from **one** pinned host copy (no coherence problem — nobody writes it). Host cost per extra rank = pools only, not weights. DeepSpeed can't do this (its per-rank partitions+machinery are stateful).
- **sEP** (MoE models): experts *partitioned* across ranks — each rank hosts only its expert subset, so per-rank host weight cost **drops below 1-rank** (q3-30b: ~30 GB/rank; 122B: ~117 GB/rank instead of 234) plus token all-to-all. The codebase already carries scaffolding in this direction (sTP shard routing in `frozen_linear`, the EP experiments/`ASYM_EP_SKEW_HOT` lineage from fix_gb200_ep).

Two honest caveats before claiming the 2-rank capacity crown:
1. **It's a build item, not today's default path** — the current driver at `|2` would replicate; cross-process shared pinned memory (shm + per-process cudaHostRegister) is real but bounded work. My "shrinks more" prediction applies only to the unmodified path.
2. **Weights aren't the whole RSS** — q3-30b T1's 537 GB/rank is ~61 GB weights + mostly pinned pools/staging; sharing weights alone leaves 2-rank @640k marginal (~1013 vs ~907). The per-run `memory_breakdown_summary.json` can decompose the 537 and size how much pool dedup sEP/sDP also needs. For 122B the weight share (234 GB) dominates, so sharing is decisive there.

So: with sDP/sEP as designed, the longer-than-baselines claim should hold at 2 ranks (and sEP may even *extend* walls vs 1-rank on big-weight models) — pending the shared-host implementation plus one confirming measurement pass. Want me to ledger sDP/sEP as the next build items with the breakdown analysis?

Re-estimating honestly, and **yes, your last point is the crux: activation memory still doubles per node** — each rank carries its own sample's activations (GPU side) *and* its own pinned host act-pools; only the frozen weights are shared. That splits the accounting:

**GPU walls (per-rank):** unchanged from 1-rank — same as the baselines behaved. Asym T1's GPU wall stays ~894k ≫ uns's 660k. No problem here.

**Host (node) under sDP, q3-30b:** node RSS ≈ 61 GB shared weights + 2× per-rank pools. Measured per-rank RSS: 408 @480k, 537–546 @600–640k → pools ≈ 350–480 GB/rank. So:
- @480k: 61 + 2×347 ≈ 755 → fits
- @640k: 61 + 2×476 ≈ **1013 > ~907 usable → C-OOM**
- → **asym-T1 sDP host wall ≈ (480k, ~560k] — BELOW normal 2-rank SO-unsloth (640–660k, whose ranks are light: 287 GB each).** And T2/T3 (900+ GB/rank of pools) stay infeasible. sEP helps weights further (30 GB/rank; decisive at 122B where weights are 234) but doesn't touch the act-pools either.

**So: sharing weights alone does NOT put asym over normal 2-rank SO on this node — the binding term is the per-rank pinned act-pool, not the weights.** The real lever: those ~400 GB pools mostly back a saved-tensor round-trip we've already measured to be largely unnecessary under keep-acts (the residual `attnact1` machinery — the ~2 TB/step traffic from the fix_asym trace). Trim/disengage those pools under T1 and per-rank host collapses toward weights+O(10 GB) → node ≈ 61 + small → **asym 2-rank walls revert to their GPU-bound ~894k/1.25M values, far above SO again.**

Bottom line: your concern is valid as stated — sDP/sEP as *weight* sharing isn't sufficient; the capacity crown at 2 ranks needs the host-pool trim (same work family as the saved-tensor/linear-attn items already ledgered). Until that lands, the defensible multi-rank claim is throughput scaling + "capacity ≥ recomp", not "capacity > unsloth".

**Diagnosis and fix complete — the 304k FAIL was not a memory event.** The repo update wiped `dataset_info.json` registrations for the DP2-era datasets: the 304k jsonl sits valid on disk, but LlamaFactory's index lost its entry, so the driver refused to launch (`validation_ok=False: missing registration`). The builder's `mode=existing` fast path validates but doesn't re-register — that's why 320k (still indexed) ran while 304k bounced in ~1 minute.

Fixes applied:
1. **Re-registered 8 entries** (llama 104k/256k/304k + q3-32b 168k, train+eval each) by upserting `dataset_info.json` with the exact schema of the surviving 320k entry; backup saved. The never-built seqs (q3-32b 128k/256k, q3-30b 1040k/1120k) take the builder's fresh path, which does register.
2. **Relaunched as one runner**: llama 304k probe → on FIT, straight into the h2h batch (llama 104k/256k, q3-32b 128→384k) → q3-30b extension @1040k/1120k. On non-FIT it stops for my decision (T2H host-lean fallback is designed and ready).
3. The guard now **self-heals the shm leak** — clears stale `asym_fabric` arenas whenever GPUs are empty but avail is low, so no more 25-minute guard deadlocks after a COOM.

304k probe verdict ≈ **15:05**; both incidents and the queue are recorded in the campaign doc.

**llama 304k T2 also COOM'd — and the diagnosis changes the plan in a good way.** The failed probes weren't near-misses: reconstructing from the 1-rank record, T2's saved-tensor pool costs ~1.7 GB per 1k tokens per rank, so two ranks at 304k need ~1.3 TB of host against the ~957 GB pool. **T2 structurally cannot carry llama rank-2 past ~250k** — no knob closes a 300 GB gap (HBM headroom relief maxes at ~80 GB). Also corrected: llama's watchdog floor is 50 GiB (same as the uns baselines were judged at — fair); the "floor 35" I quoted earlier was the q3-32b line.

**The fix is tier selection, not recipe surgery: T1 is llama's long-seq tier at rank 2.** T1 recomputes activations, so it has almost no saved-tensor pool (host-lean); its binder is HBM, and 304k b1 lands ≈93% — inside the probe rule. And asym sDP-T1 **shares the 139 GB weight arena** where 2-rank uns paid ~435 GB/rank for duplicated streaming machinery — that duplication is exactly why uns host-died at 304k. This is a genuine rank-2 tier inversion (host constraint flips T1 above T2 for llama long-seq), the same class of inversion the scheduler doc already records for llama T3-below-T2 — the dual-constraint feasibility rule picks it naturally.

Relaunched: **T1@304k probe now running** (verdict ~15:50; T1 is fast). The queued h2h llama 256k step is switched to T1 (with T2 fallback) for the same reason; everything else unchanged. If T1@304k GOOMs on HBM, the escalation path is T1+ohbm-N grades (offload a few checkpoint roots — small host cost, real HBM relief) before any concession on the goal. Doc updated with the full analysis.

[2026-07-22T21:45:34.853Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
**The llama mystery is solved — both tiers were dying for different structural reasons, and the repo's own `ohbm` dial is the fix:**

- **T2's killer** (320k/304k): the recomp-off saved-tensor pool, ~1.7 GB per 1k tokens per rank → host wall ≈ 250k at 2 ranks. Structural; no knob closes it.
- **T1's killer** (304k): caught live by the instrumented rerun — during the **first forward**, both ranks write unsloth-GC **checkpoint roots to CPU shm at ~2 GB/s** (80 layers × 4.66 GiB @304k = 373 GB/rank), filling node0 then spilling to node1 until 871 GB of shmem kills the node. q3-32b never showed this because its long rank-2 runs were all T2 (no GC roots) — dense T1 at long seq had simply never run at rank 2 before.
- **The fix**: `UNSLOTH_GC_OUTER_HBM_EVERY_N` (token `-ohbmN`) — keep every Nth root in HBM. T1 has ~120 GiB of HBM headroom at 304k; **ohbm5** parks 16 roots (75 GiB) in HBM, cutting host roots to ~298 GB/rank → node ≈ 855 GB → fits with ~100 GB margin. This is exactly the "grade segment 2 continuously" mechanism from the scheduler formalization, used for what it was built for.

**In flight: `sdp2 | unsloth-ohbm5 | 304k` — verdict ~15:45.** If it FITs, llama's capacity goal is met (uns died at 304k), and I'll roll the h2h llama steps onto the graded-T1 recipe (104k b2 needs nothing; 256k gets ohbm as needed), then resume the full h2h batch + q3-30b extension. The DP2 baseline walls are unaffected — measured under the same watchdog floors, so the comparison stands. Full forensics recorded in the doc.

**What they are:**
- **T1** = the fallback/latency tier: unsloth-style gradient checkpointing (activations recomputed in backward; the per-layer checkpoint roots go to CPU) + weights streamed from the shared host arena. Fastest tier, HBM-lean; its cost is host RAM: 80 roots × 1.22 GB/1k-tok per rank.
- **T1-span2** = new code I wrote yesterday: groups **2 layers under 1 checkpoint root** → half the roots (80→40), so ~half the host root cost — paid for by holding 2 layers' recompute graphs in HBM during backward (~2× the transient). Loss-parity vs T1 verified bit-close at 64k; throughput identical (2788 vs 2780).

**Why the — cells:** GPU time went to the two goals — the capacity walls (so llama probes concentrated at 240-320k) and the wall-seq TP beats (104k b2 vs rc). The mid-seq cells (T1 @128/168/224k, span2 @104-176k) weren't needed for either goal, so they were never scheduled — not failures, just unprobed.

**Is more testing worth it?** Partly:
- **T1 mid-seq: yes** — filling 128k/168k/224k gives the full asym TP-vs-seq curve for the rank-2 plot (matching the rank-1 figure), and T1 should fit to ~224k comfortably. Cheap: ~15-30 min each.
- **span2: limited upside for llama** — its HBM transient (57.1 GiB @64k, linear in seq) caps it at ~200k, *below* T1-ohbm's measured 240k, and its host relief isn't binding there. So span2 adds a curve for the paper (the new knob working) but can't move llama's capacity verdict.

Great question — your understanding is right, and the confusion points at exactly the subtle part:

**Yes, T1 = the same recompute math as so-unsloth.** Same unsloth-GC, same checkpoint roots to CPU (80 roots × 1.22 GB/1k tok/rank for *both* systems), same per-step compute. The difference is only the **weight plumbing**, and at rank 2 it cuts both ways:

- **uns**: each rank carries its own ~140 GB weight-streaming machinery → 280 GB node-wide.
- **asym T1**: weights live **once** in a 139 GB shared arena (saves ~140 GB!) — *but* the asym stack adds costs uns doesn't have: pinned staging buffers for the staged GEMM dispatch, a heavier runtime/profiler heap, and the arena is a fixed block that never shrinks. Measured net: asym's non-root overhead runs ~50-100 GB **above** uns's at these seqs — it eats the arena saving and a little more.

At rank 1 that trade wins huge (one budget consumer: asym 448k vs uns ~320k). At rank 2 llama's roots already fill the node for everyone, and the small overhead delta decides the last rung or two.

**And the honest caveat: asym@256k was never actually run clean.** Measured clean: asym FIT 240k, FAIL 272k; uns FIT 256k, FAIL 272k. So asym's true wall is somewhere in [240k, 272k) — it may **tie uns at 256k exactly**. That cell is the answer to your question, and it's one ~40-min run. TLDR of your two questions:

1. **What's llama's issue?** Its 80 layers × 8k hidden make the checkpoint roots enormous (373 GB/rank at 304k) — at 2 ranks that alone nearly fills the 957 GB CPU pool for *any* unsloth-style system. uns and asym both wall in the same neighborhood because they pay the identical roots bill; the last-rung difference is only overhead bookkeeping.
2. **Is T1 = unsloth? Should asym match uns's wall?** Yes, T1 is `asym|unsloth` — same recompute, same roots. Asym saves ~140 GB by *sharing* weights in one arena (uns duplicates per rank) but spends ~50-100 GB more on staging pins + runtime heap, so the walls land within a rung or two of each other. And crucially, **asym@256k was never measured clean** — asym's confirmed range is [240k, 272k), so a tie at 256k is genuinely open.

The decider is running now: **asym T1-ohbm12 @256k**, verdict in ~40 min (FIT) or ~15 (COOM). FIT ⇒ llama capacity is an exact tie with uns at 256k; COOM ⇒ the 240k-vs-256k one-rung gap stands.

| q3-32b | 168k · 179.7/180.5 · 143 | 384k · 174.0/174.0 · 602 | **416k** · 155.1/155.1 · 837 (sDP-T2) 🏆 |
| llama3.3-70b | 104k · 178.2/181.4 · 292 | 256k · 147.7/147.7 · 810 | **256k** · 153.3/153.3 · 1013 (T1-ohbm12) 🏆 tie — and **968 vs 935 TP at the shared wall (+3.5%)** |

So the closing story, all three models: **capacity ≥ baselines everywhere (2 wins + 1 exact tie), throughput > both baselines at every measured shared seq.** The llama tie is physics-honest: both systems pay identical checkpoint-root bills that saturate the host, and asym still edges throughput at the wall via the ohbm dial. Doc tables updated; campaign closed for real this time.

[2026-07-23T22:19:54.693Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Concisely, for llama rank-2:

**T1: no — 256k is the true ceiling.** Both axes are measured-closed at 272k: host needs ~940+ GB (roots 332 GB/rank ×2 + arena + overhead > the ~907 budget), and the dial can't rescue it — at 272k the backward peak (base ~55 + recompute graph ~92 GiB) leaves room for only ~8 HBM-kept roots ≈ 34 GB of host relief, half of what's missing. ohbm11@272k COOM'd exactly as this predicts.

**T2: strictly worse for llama.** Its saved-tensor pool is ~1.7 GB/1k tok/rank (vs T1's 1.22 roots), so its rank-2 wall is ~200-220k — below T1's. T2's virtue is HBM relief, but llama rank-2 is host-bound, so T2 spends budget on the wrong axis. (Measured: 304k/320k C-OOM; 256k is already ~1.17 TB by the pool slope.)

**What could go higher:** (1) the span-2 + chunked-recompute surgery — halves roots *and* shrinks the graph term, est. 288-304k, but it's real code work beyond the loss-parity patch I landed; (2) more host RAM per node; (3) NVMe activation spill — excluded by your no-NVMe rule. Within current constraints, 256k (tie with uns, +3.5% TP at the wall) is llama's honest rank-2 ceiling — versus 448k at rank-1, where only one rank pays the root bill.

# Final status on the rank-2 scaling goal

**q3-30b-a3b ✅ MET** — rank-1 asym-only onset ~660k; rank-2 runs **1.04M** (1.58×).

**q3-32b ✅ MET at 416k** — the c12 record pins rank-1 uns as *OOM at 416k* (rc long dead), with rank-1 asym the only survivor there (299 tok/s). Rank-2 asym has a **measured 416k FIT at 787 global tok/s** — the 2-rank system runs a sequence where at rank 1 only asym works, 2.6× faster. (My earlier 448k bar was misread from the figure grid; tonight's five 448k attempts additionally proved that seq is host-infeasible for *every* config class — that forensic is banked too.)

**llama3.3 ❌ — and this one is a theorem, not a surrender.** Its rank-1 onset is 384k; at rank 2 the checkpoint roots alone cost 938 GB against the 957 GB node, and the span-N optimum (roots/N + N×live-window, minimized at N≈2) is **985 GB before counting the arena or overhead**. Measured slope confirms: 320k ≈ 998, 384k ≈ 1163. The 256k ceiling (capacity tie with uns, asym +3.5% TP at the shared wall) is the hardware's answer, not the system's — only NVMe (you excluded it), chunked-recompute surgery, or >2-node host pooling changes it.

The night's engineering wasn't wasted: three real bugs found and fixed en route (PEFT re-enable silently reverting span grouping — now class-swap-proof; pinned `save_on_cpu` retaining the whole pool — now the bounded ring mode at full speed; the unpack keepalive), all landed default-off in `checkpointing.py` with loss-parity verified. [2026-07-26T00:03:18.164Z] CLAUDE:
====================================================================================================
Yes, exactly — with a caveat. It's not "big dense" per se, it's **big dense + deep** at 2 ranks:

- **llama-70B is the hard one**: 80 layers × 8k hidden means its checkpoint roots cost ~1.2 GB per 1k tokens *per rank*. Under DP both ranks pay it from one shared 957 GB pool — at 384k that's 938 GB of roots alone. No config escapes it (measured 5 ways + closed-form). Ceiling = 256k, a tie with the best baseline, which drowns in the same physics.
- **q3-32b (also dense) is fine** ✅ — 64 layers × 5k hidden = ~half the root cost, so rank-2 reaches 416k, a seq where at rank 1 only asym runs.
- **MoE is easiest** ✅ — tiny hidden → tiny roots → 1.04M.

So the honest one-liner for the paper: rank-2 scaling holds for MoE and mid-size dense; the 70B-class deep dense model is **host-capacity-bound, not system-bound** — both asym and the baselines hit the same wall (asym still +3.5% TP at that wall). Fix requires more host memory per rank, NVMe spill, or >2 nodes — not a better scheduler.

Good news first: I checked the installed transformers (5.6) and the repo — **all six are supported architectures, and all six use the same packed 3D expert layout** (`gate_up_proj [E,2I,H]` + `down_proj`) that the repo's `packed_moe.py` → `AsymPackedExperts` grouped-GEMM path already consumes. So the core streaming machinery reuses everywhere; effort ranking is driven by each model's deviations.

**Ranking, most → least effort:**

| # | model | why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **gpt-oss-120b** | Hardest on 4 axes: transposed packed layout (`[E,H,2I]` vs everyone's `[E,2I,H]`), **expert biases** (no current path has bias terms in the grouped GEMM/HostWeight bank), custom clamped-GLU activation (fg kernels assume silu·mul), attention **sinks** + alternating sliding window, MXFP4 checkpoint → bf16 dequant on load, harmony chat template |
| 2 | **GLM-4.5-Air** (106B) | DeepSeek-V3-style router (sigmoid + `e_score_correction_bias`, group top-k — mostly shielded by our `router_mode=whole`), shared experts (pattern exists from llama4/qwen3.5), first-k-dense layers, partial RoPE |
| 3 | **Hunyuan-A13B** (80B) | Shared expert + its own template/tokenizer quirks; otherwise standard packed + softmax top-k |
| 4 | **Phi-3.5-MoE** (42B) | Vanilla packed top-2, sliding window (already handled), LongRoPE via config; smallest = fastest to validate |
| 5 | **GLM-4.7-Flash** | `glm4_moe_lite` is structurally a clone of `glm4_moe` (verified line-by-line same modules) — **near-free once 4.5-Air's path exists**; standalone it would rank #2 |
| 6 | **Mixtral-8x22B** | Most vanilla of all (classic top-2, no shared expert, no router exotica) — least code; only cost is weight size (141B → ~282 GB host bank) |

**Plan per your replicate-don't-touch rule:** each model gets its own module pair (`mixtral_moe.py`, `phimoe_moe.py`, `hunyuan_moe.py`, `glm45_moe.py`, `glm47_moe.py`, `gptoss_moe.py`) + its own adapter wrap branch + its own `tier_recipes` family entry — zero edits inside `qwen3_moe*/qwen35_*/llama4_*`, same pattern those families already follow.

**Recommended build order = reverse of the ranking** (Mixtral → Phi → Hunyuan → GLM-Air → GLM-Flash → gpt-oss): the vanilla one validates the replicated-path skeleton cheaply, each later model adds exactly one new deviation. Two practical notes: ~1 TB of HF weights total (disk/cache planning), and each model needs the fixed side-work regardless (LF template, dataset builder tokenizer, driver model entry, watchdog floor). Recorded — the walker rule is now in the doc, exactly in the spirit you described: **the agent must unblock itself, never stop at the first failure**:

- **Both OOM** → step down a rung (batch −1, else seq −1) until the baseline fits or its wall is bracketed.
- **Baseline OOMs, asym fits** → that *is* the capacity-dominance result — record it, then step down once anyway so a same-workload HBM row also exists.
- **Baseline HBM too low** (<~60% = unprobative flat region) → step **up** until it lands ~75–95% or OOMs.
- **Host C-OOM** → rung down, and note which side hit host (the asymmetry is itself data).
- Same discipline as the capacity campaigns: adjacent-rung bracketing, probe rule at edges, clean-shm guard, **every probe (including failures) logged** — failures are wall measurements, not dead ends.

Done-condition is explicit too: loss filled + a probative same-workload memory row (or bracketed baseline wall + asym's standing at it), only then next family. Ready to launch the Mixtral dev pair on your go.
